questions.text: Which of the following cells derived from the lymphoid lineage?
questions.explanation: NK cells share lymphoid ancestry with T and B lymphocytes; the other listed cells are myeloid.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered a professional antigen-presenting cell?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells process antigen and present peptide-MHC complexes to activate T cells.

questions.text: Dendritic cells, macrophages and ______ are professional antigen-presenting cells to T helper lymphocytes.
questions.explanation: B cells internalize antigen through their surface immunoglobulin and present peptides on MHC class II to helper T cells.

questions.text: Which cells are functionally deficient in a person with a genetic defect in perforins and granzymes?
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells and NK cells both use cytotoxic granules to induce target-cell apoptosis; a shared granule defect affects both.

questions.text: Which of the following types of cells are notable for their presence at the sites of helminth infections?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are especially associated with responses against helminths and are recruited to sites of parasitic infection.

questions.text: NK cells are members of which of the following families of leukocytes?
questions.explanation: NK cells develop from lymphoid progenitors and form a population of granular innate lymphocytes.

questions.text: Which one of the following cells has both characters of specificity and memory?
questions.explanation: B cells have antigen-specific receptors and can generate memory cells after activation. The other listed cells are conventional innate populations.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a cell developed from the myeloid stem cell
questions.explanation: NK cells arise from lymphoid lineage; red cells, neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages arise from myeloid progenitors.

questions.text: which of the following cells can phagocytose other cells but in the tissue
questions.explanation: Macrophages are tissue phagocytes, while monocytes circulate in blood.

questions.text: Talk about the the cells that can be develop from pluripotent cell
questions.modelAnswer: Hematopoietic stem cells give rise to myeloid and lymphoid progenitors. Myeloid branches generate erythrocytes, megakaryocytes/platelets, granulocytes, monocytes/macrophages and related antigen-presenting/tissue cells. Lymphoid branches generate B cells, T cells and NK cells. B cells mature primarily in bone marrow, while T-cell precursors mature in thymus.

questions.text: Which of the following leukocytes increase in number in case of helminths "parasite" infections & allergy
questions.explanation: Helminth infection and allergy characteristically raise eosinophils; neutrophils and macrophages serve different dominant functions.

questions.text: When monocytes migrate to tissue and leave blood, they are called
questions.explanation: Circulating monocytes differentiate into tissue macrophages; CTLs and NK cells are separate lymphoid lineages.

questions.text: T lymphocytes are
options: Can ingest pathogens and kill them
Can recirculate through the blood and lymphoid organs
Are educated in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: T cells recirculate through blood and lymphoid tissue, do not ordinarily phagocytose, can be long-lived, and mature in thymus.

questions.text: Where are lymphocytes activated by antigen?
questions.explanation: Naive lymphocytes encounter antigen and become activated in secondary lymphoid organs, including lymph nodes.

questions.text: The largest lymphoid organ that clears Particulate matter from blood and concentrates blood-borne pathogens is the:
questions.explanation: The spleen filters blood and captures blood-borne antigens; lymph nodes filter lymph.

questions.text: The role of central or Primary lymphoid organs in the immune system is:
options: Exposing T cells to foreign antigens
Primary site for antibody synthesis and release
Filter blood and trap foreign blood- bome antigens
Provide the microenvironment for maturation of B and T cells
Line the mucosal surfaces of the body for efficient antigen contact
questions.explanation: Primary lymphoid organs provide the environment for B-cell maturation in bone marrow and T-cell maturation in thymus.

questions.text: Cells are obtained from a primary lymphoid organ of a mouse as a part of a research project. From which of the following organs were these cells isolated?
questions.explanation: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where developing T lymphocytes mature; lymph nodes, spleen and Peyer’s patches are secondary organs.

questions.text: The primary lymphoid organs are those in which
options: Adaptive immune responses are usually initiated
Large number of circulating lymphocytes make contact with one another
questions.explanation: Initial lymphocyte development and maturation take place in primary lymphoid organs. Foreign antigen-driven activation normally begins in secondary lymphoid tissues.

questions.text: Secondary lymphoid organs are sites in which
options: Adaptive immune responses are usually initiated
questions.explanation: Secondary lymphoid organs bring antigens, antigen-presenting cells and mature lymphocytes together to initiate adaptive responses.

questions.text: An organ that acts as a filter to remove cellular debris and microorganisms from lymph prior to its return to the circulatory system is
questions.explanation: Afferent lymph enters lymph nodes, where antigens and debris are trapped before lymph returns toward the circulation.

questions.text: The thymus is the site of initial differentiation of
questions.explanation: T-cell precursors originate in marrow and migrate to the thymus to mature. B cells mature primarily in bone marrow.

questions.text: The cytokine that favors development of lymphoid precursors in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: IL-7 supplied by stromal cells supports developing lymphoid cells, including B-lineage precursors in bone marrow.

questions.text: List the primary and secondary lymphoid organs with their function
questions.modelAnswer: Primary organs: bone marrow generates blood cells and matures B cells; thymus selects/matures T cells. Secondary organs: lymph nodes collect tissue lymph antigens; spleen samples blood antigens; MALT including tonsils and Peyer patches samples mucosal antigens. These bring antigen and lymphocytes together for activation.
questions.explanation: Primary organs: bone marrow generates blood cells and matures B cells; thymus selects/matures T cells. Secondary organs: lymph nodes collect tissue lymph antigens; spleen samples blood antigens; MALT including tonsils and Peyer patches samples mucosal antigens. These bring antigen and lymphocytes together for activation.

questions.text: Function of bone marrow include all of the following except
questions.explanation: T cells mature in thymus; bone marrow generates blood cells and matures B cells.

questions.text: Which of the following lymphoid organs is considered lymph filter?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes filter lymph; spleen filters blood and mucosal tissues sample local antigens.

subjects.lectures: Inflammation and leukocyte recruitment, Innate barriers and recognition, NK cells and antiviral interferons, Phagocytosis and killing

questions.text: In addition to IL- 1, which of the following is an inflammation-inducing cytokine?
questions.explanation: TNF-α is a major inflammatory cytokine made by activated macrophages, alongside IL-1 and IL-6.

questions.text: Which of the following adhesion molecules is expressed on endothelial lining of blood vessels near an active focus of infection to mediate rolling of neutrophils on vasculature as a first step to reach the infection site?
questions.explanation: Endothelial E-selectin mediates neutrophil rolling. Integrin binding to ICAM supports subsequent firm adhesion.

questions.text: A patient with acute appendicitis had a temperature of 39°C and a blood leukocyte count of 20,000 cells/µL. The predominant cell type in his blood is:
questions.explanation: Acute pyogenic inflammation commonly produces neutrophilic leukocytosis as neutrophils are recruited from marrow and blood pools.

questions.text: A cell utilizing reactive O₂ species and lysosomal enzymes to kill pathogens is:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils kill ingested pathogens using a respiratory burst and granule/lysosomal enzymes. Cytotoxic lymphocytes primarily attack host target cells.

questions.text: All of the following are acute-phase proteins EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Histamine is a small inflammatory amine released by mast cells, not a hepatic acute-phase protein. CRP, mannose-binding lectin, fibrinogen and serum amyloid A are acute-phase proteins.

questions.text: Neutrophils are attracted to sites of infection by:
questions.explanation: C5a and CXCL8 (IL-8) recruit and activate neutrophils. C3b principally serves as an opsonin rather than this chemotactic signal.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines acts an endogenous pyrogen?
questions.explanation: IL-1 is an endogenous pyrogen. Together with TNF-α and IL-6, it mediates systemic inflammatory responses including fever.

questions.text: All of the following cytokines induce an acute phase response EXCEPT
questions.explanation: IL-1, TNF-α and IL-6 stimulate the hepatic acute-phase response. IL-2 principally supports lymphocyte proliferation.

questions.text: Three days ago, an otherwise healthy individual sustained a skin laceration during a football match. Yesterday he began to complain of flu like symptoms. This morning he became suddenly ill with high fever, general muscle aches and dizziness then he lost consciousness. On arrival to the emergency department, he had a temperature of 39.5°C and a heart rate of 136 beat/minute. His blood leukocyte count was 12,500 per μl. The predominant cell type(s) in this patient’s blood is/are most likely
questions.explanation: Acute pyogenic infection mobilizes circulating mature and immature neutrophils.

questions.text: All of the following characterise the process of inflammation except
options: Vasodilation occurs by increasing the diameter of the vessel
Vascular permeability to make cell reach the site of inflammation
Migration of WBCs occurs to kill the pathogen
questions.explanation: Acute inflammation involves vasodilation, permeability and leukocyte migration; sustained vasoconstriction is not the stated canonical response.

questions.text: Mention the pro-inflammatory cytokines that produced by WBCs
questions.modelAnswer: Name principal acute inflammatory leukocyte cytokines TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6, with IL-8/CXCL8 recruiting neutrophils and IL-12 supporting Th1/NK responses. Explain local endothelial activation/recruitment and systemic fever, marrow leukocytosis and hepatic acute-phase production.
questions.explanation: Name principal acute inflammatory leukocyte cytokines TNF-α, IL-1 and IL-6, with IL-8/CXCL8 recruiting neutrophils and IL-12 supporting Th1/NK responses. Explain local endothelial activation/recruitment and systemic fever, marrow leukocytosis and hepatic acute-phase production.

questions.text: which of the following cell is the first cell that phagocytose of bacteria
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited and are the principal early phagocytes in acute bacterial inflammation.

questions.text: All of the following cytokines are involved in acute inflammatory reactions except
questions.explanation: IL-2 is chiefly a T-cell growth cytokine; IL-1, IL-6 and TNF drive acute inflammation.

questions.text: Pro inflammatory cytokines play an important role in inflammation as they:
options: Induce WBCs recruitment to the site of infection
Induce liver production of CRP and MBL
questions.explanation: Inflammatory cytokines recruit leukocytes, mobilize marrow cells, and induce hepatic acute-phase proteins.

questions.text: A cytokine produced by macrophage that induce expression of adhesion molecules by endothelial cells is called
questions.explanation: IL-1 activates endothelium; TGF-β is mainly regulatory and IL-4 and IL-17 serve other dominant functions.

questions.text: Tissue damage and entry of pathogenic organisms trigger a sequence of reactions known as:
questions.explanation: Infection and tissue damage initiate inflammation, not simply opsonization or antigen-specific clonal expansion.

questions.text: Concerning systemic protective effects of pro inflammatory cytokines, they include all of the following except:
options: Effect on bone marrow causing leukocytosis
Effect on blood vessels causing vascular leakage and thrombosis
questions.explanation: Fever, leukocytosis and acute-phase production can protect; extensive vascular leak and thrombosis represent harmful systemic inflammation.

questions.text: A 66 years old man came to the clinic complaining of an abscess on his neck, which of the following mediators does not contribute in recruitment and extravasation of neutrophils to the site of his infection?
questions.explanation: IFN-γ primarily activates macrophages; TNF, IL-1, IL-8 and C5a support inflammatory neutrophil recruitment.

questions.text: What is the cell-surface molecule that play the key role of recognizing a foreign antigen by macrophages?
questions.explanation: Toll-like receptors are innate pattern-recognition receptors sensing microbial components and triggering macrophage responses.

questions.text: Which of the following is a specific defense against a pathogen?
questions.explanation: Antibodies provide antigen-specific humoral defence; the other listed mechanisms are innate effectors.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences correctly defines Bacteriocins?
options: Enzymes present in the lysozomes of macrophages
Inhibitory substances released from normal bacterial flora
questions.explanation: Bacteriocins are bacterial inhibitory products that can restrict other microbes and contribute to colonization resistance.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE regarding innate and adaptive immunity?
options: They cooperate together to prevent and eliminate infections
They are fast in their response
questions.explanation: Innate sensing and APC activation initiate adaptive responses, and adaptive antibodies and T cells recruit innate effectors.

questions.text: All of the following are Pattern Recognition Receptors except
questions.explanation: Fc receptors recognize the constant region of antibodies rather than directly identifying microbial molecular patterns.

questions.text: Non mammalian epitopes on the surface of microorganisms that differ from those on human cells are called
questions.explanation: PAMPs are conserved microbial structures recognized by innate pattern-recognition molecules. DAMPs instead arise from stressed or injured host cells.

questions.text: All of the following are examples of Pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Defensins are host antimicrobial peptides. The other options describe microbial structures that can act as PAMPs.

questions.text: All of the following are members of innate immunity except:
questions.explanation: Skin, tears, mucociliary clearance and resident flora provide innate barriers. Antigen-specific IgG is produced by B cells as part of adaptive humoral immunity, even though innate phagocytes use it for opsonization.

questions.text: A 23 year old female patient developed vaginal candidiasis after recovery from a urinary bladder infection caused by E coli. The most likely explanation for development of this fungal infection is:
options: Movement of fungi from her urinary bladder to her vagina
Antibiotic-induced reduction in vaginal commensal bacteria
Decreased vaginal pH resulting from the recent infection
Increased vaginal mucus secretion following antibiotic therapy
Overgrowth of Lactobacilli in cervical os
questions.explanation: Antibiotics disrupt commensal bacterial competition, permitting Candida overgrowth.

questions.text: A 36 year old female patient is diagnosed with septicemia. Blood culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae. This patient’s initial immune response will involve
options: Binding of somatically generated receptors to Klebsiella pneumoniae
Recognition of LPS by toll-like receptors
Stimulation of the classical complement pathway
questions.explanation: Initial LPS sensing uses germline-encoded Toll-like receptors.

questions.text: A 23 year old female who has never been vaccinated against seasonal influenza is exposed to an influenza virus. Which of the following structures allow cells of her innate immune system to attempt to prevent infection and illness?
questions.explanation: Innate recognition uses conserved microbial patterns.

questions.text: A 34 year old female diabetic patient developed a Staph aureus infection. Which of the following structures expressed by cells of the innate immune system enable them to recognize the bacteria?
questions.explanation: Innate immune cells sense bacterial patterns through pattern-recognition receptors.

questions.text: A 4 year old boy had consumed a peanut butter sandwich contaminated by garden soil (mud) while playing in the garden of his house. Despite the presence of several species of bacteria within the soil, the boy’s intestine was not colonized by the ingested bacteria. The most likely explanation for that is:
options: Acid in the stomach kills the bacteria before they enter the intestine
IgE produced in response to peanut ingestion inhibits the growth of the bacteria
Unfavorable environmental conditions kills the bacteria before he eats them
Soil bacteria are digested and quickly eliminated along with food
Starch in bread he ate kills the bacteria in his gut
questions.explanation: Gastric acidity is an innate chemical barrier against ingested organisms.

questions.text: All of the following characterize the innate immunity except
questions.explanation: Antibody generation is adaptive; classical innate immunity is initial, pattern-based and lacks conventional antigen-specific memory.

questions.text: All of the following are chemical barriers except
options: It has a keratin layer to prevent entry of organism
It has an HCl to make a complete lysis of organism
It contains saliva which contains enzymes induce lysis of the organism
It contains sweat which has salt that cause lysis of the organism
questions.explanation: Keratin is a physical barrier; acid, salivary antimicrobials and sweat components are chemical defenses.

questions.text: Which of the following are true about flora
options: Compete with pathogenic organism to inhibit the attachment
Compete with pathogenic organism about the food
It produces bacteriocins which cause inhibit or kill the other bacteria
questions.explanation: Commensals compete for niches/nutrients and may produce inhibitory bacteriocins.

questions.text: All of the following are examples of PAMP except?
questions.explanation: Defensins are host antimicrobial peptides; microbial LPS, nucleic acids and teichoic acids can serve as PAMPs.

questions.text: Neutrophils recognize their target using
questions.explanation: PRRs detect microbial patterns; C5a directs chemotaxis and Fc receptors detect opsonizing antibody.

questions.text: Normal microbiota "Flora" can participate in formation of innate immunity barriers as they:
options: Enhance leukocytes migration to the site of infection
questions.explanation: Commensals compete with pathogens for colonization niches and nutrients.

questions.text: In the standard introductory comparison with adaptive immunity, which of the following is characteristic of conventional innate responses?
options: Each receptor binds to one specific organism
It responds slowly the first time it recognizes an invading pathogen
It includes both B and T cells
They act rapidly without first requiring antigen-specific clonal expansion
questions.explanation: Conventional innate responses use pre-existing germline-encoded recognition systems and act rapidly. Adaptive B- and T-cell responses require antigen-specific activation and clonal expansion. Trained innate responses can change later responsiveness, so equal effectiveness on every exposure is not an absolute rule.

questions.text: Innate immunity involves all except
questions.explanation: Antibodies are products of adaptive B cells; barriers, phagocytosis and inflammation are innate mechanisms.

questions.text: Which of the following is a correct statement about NK cells?
options: They kill target cells by phagocytosis and intracellular digestion
They are a subset of polymorphonuclear cells
They are particularly effective against certain bacteria
They kill target cells in an extracellular fashion
They proliferate in response to antigen
questions.explanation: NK cells kill susceptible target cells by releasing cytotoxic granules across an intercellular contact, rather than ingesting them.

questions.text: Which of the following cells is a constituent of innate immunity?
questions.explanation: NK cells are innate lymphocytes that act early against infected or abnormal cells without requiring a clonally rearranged T-cell receptor.

questions.text: Which of the following immune cells are able to recognize cells with depressed levels of MHC class I proteins on their surface?
questions.explanation: Reduced MHC class I expression removes inhibitory signals from NK cells, increasing susceptibility to their cytotoxic attack.

questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding NK cells?
options: They proliferate in response to antigen
They kill their target cells by phagocytosis and intracellular digestion
They are a subset of T cytotoxic cells
They kill their targets by perforins and granzymes stored in their granules
They are particularly effective against extracellular bacteria
questions.explanation: NK cells release cytotoxic granules onto target cells to induce apoptosis; their killing is not phagocytosis.

questions.text: The major source of early IFN-γ in the immune response is:
questions.explanation: NK cells supply IFN-γ early, before antigen-specific T-cell responses develop. Later, Th1 and cytotoxic T cells also contribute.

questions.text: IFN-γ produced by NK cells early in the immune response activates ______, which in turn produces ______, activating NK cells.
questions.explanation: Macrophage IL-12 activates NK cells, which release IFN-γ to enhance macrophage activity, forming an early antimicrobial feedback loop.

questions.text: Which of the following statements describes a NK cell?
options: An innate immune cell that attacks pathogens by pattern recognition receptors
An innate immune cell that acts early in viral infection by secreting IFN-γ
A specialized cell that kills virally infected cells expressing the viral peptide in association with MHC class I
An innate immune cells that recognize pathogen by a receptor specific for antigen
An adaptive immune cell that recognizes virally infected cells expressing low levels of MHC class
questions.explanation: NK cells act during early antiviral immunity and release IFN-γ. Antigen-specific peptide-MHC recognition is characteristic of cytotoxic T cells.

questions.text: What is the ligand that binds to inhibitory receptors on NK cells?
questions.explanation: Normal MHC class I molecules engage inhibitory NK receptors, helping protect healthy self cells from NK-mediated killing.

questions.text: An immune cell which recognizes body cells with reduced expression of MHC class I molecules
questions.explanation: NK cells detect loss of self MHC class I inhibitory signaling, unlike CD8 T cells that require peptide-MHC I recognition.

questions.text: Which of the following is an important criterion of alpha interferon?
options: Induce an anti-viral state infected cells only
Synthesized early in infection within virally infected cells
Part of adaptive cell mediated immune response in viral infection
Important early defense mechanism against extracellular bacteria
questions.explanation: Type I interferons are produced early during viral infection and induce an antiviral state in infected and nearby uninfected cells.

questions.text: Which of the following statements BEST describes the phenotype of a NK cell?
options: A subset of lymphocytes CD16+, CD56+ with granules containing major basic protein
A subtype of CD8+ T cytotoxic cells with granules containing perforins and granzymes
A kind of lymphocyte CD16+. CD56+, and having a receptor against MHC class I
A kind of phagocytic cell with monocyte marker having PRRs against PAMPs
A T cell with a γδ TCR found predominantly at mucosal surfaces.
questions.explanation: NK cells are granular innate lymphocytes commonly identified by CD56 and CD16. Their inhibitory receptors recognize self MHC class I; they are neither CD8 T cells nor monocyte-derived phagocytes.

questions.text: A 4 year old male presents with symptoms of febrile respiratory disease caused by Respiratory syncytial virus. NK cells of the patient detect virally infected cells by:
options: Decreased expression of PAMPs on infected cells
Decreased expression on MHC class I on virally infected cells
Increase expression of PRRs (Pattern recognition receptors) on virally infected cells
Increased expression of somatically generated receptors on NK cells
Secretion of virus specific antibodies by NK cells
questions.explanation: Reduced MHC I removes inhibitory signaling to NK cells.

questions.text: Natural killer secretes all of the following except
questions.explanation: NK cells release perforin, granzymes and IFN-γ; collagenase is not their defining cytotoxic product.

questions.text: Which of the following cells is part of innate immunity and defend against malignant or viral infected cell
questions.explanation: NK cells are innate killers of virus-infected and malignant cells; the other granulocytes have different main effector tasks.

questions.text: Which of the following characterise the IFN
options: It's secreted from viral infected cell
It causes decrease in expression of viral proteins
It causes increase in expression of MHC protein
questions.explanation: Type I IFN from infected cells inhibits viral protein synthesis and upregulates MHC-I.

questions.text: Which of the following innate immunity cells can play a role in extracellular killing of virally infected cells and tumor cells
questions.explanation: NK cells are innate cytotoxic lymphocytes; CTLs are adaptive and eosinophils target large parasites.

questions.text: Which of the following cell types of the innate immune system does not perform phagocytosis?
questions.explanation: Basophils chiefly degranulate; neutrophils, macrophages and immature dendritic cells phagocytose.

questions.text: A cell directed by IFN-γ to promote reactive O₂ species production and cytolysis is:
questions.explanation: IFN-γ activates macrophage antimicrobial functions, including increased reactive oxygen-mediated killing.

questions.text: All of the following is true about phagocytosis except
options: The phagocyte attaches to the pathogen by Toll like receptor
The phagocyte recognizes the foreign organism by PAMPs
The phagocyte causes complete lysis if it doesn't contain MHC class 2 like neutrophil
The phagocyte causes oxidative lysis by collagenase
questions.explanation: Oxidative microbial killing uses respiratory-burst products, not collagenase; TLR/PAMP recognition and phagolysosome formation aid phagocytosis.

questions.text: Compare between the fate of the phagocytosed organism in neutrophil and macrophage
questions.modelAnswer: Both neutrophils and macrophages ingest microbes into phagosomes and destroy them after lysosome fusion using oxidative and nonoxidative mechanisms. Neutrophils are short-lived recruited effectors and often die after intense killing. Macrophages are longer-lived, clear debris and dead neutrophils, secrete cytokines and present processed peptide-MHC-II to helper T cells; IFN-γ enhances killing. Avoid an absolute rule that one always completely digests and the other always preserves an organism.
questions.explanation: Both neutrophils and macrophages ingest microbes into phagosomes and destroy them after lysosome fusion using oxidative and nonoxidative mechanisms. Neutrophils are short-lived recruited effectors and often die after intense killing. Macrophages are longer-lived, clear debris and dead neutrophils, secrete cytokines and present processed peptide-MHC-II to helper T cells; IFN-γ enhances killing. Avoid an absolute rule that one always completely digests and the other always preserves an organism.

questions.text: Which of the following sentences is correct regarding phagocytosis
options: Can be stimulated by Ag coated by complement or antibody
Extracellular killing is one of the steps
questions.explanation: Antibody/complement opsonization enhances phagocytosis; innate uptake is not antigen-clonal and digestion is intracellular.

questions.text: Which of the following isn't a step of phagocytosis
options: Recognition of bacterial antigen using a specific receptor
Recognition of bacterial PAMP using PRR
questions.explanation: Innate recognition uses pattern receptors, followed by ingestion and intracellular killing; a clonally specific antigen receptor is not required.

questions.text: Functions of macrophage include:
questions.explanation: Macrophages ingest microbes, present antigen, and secrete cytokines.

subjects.name: Microbiology
subjects.lectures: Antigens, immunogens and epitopes, Haptens and superantigens, MHC structure, genetics and presentation

questions.text: The smallest unit of an antigen that is capable of binding with antibodies is
questions.explanation: An epitope is the specific antigenic determinant recognized by an antibody. The paratope is the corresponding binding site on the antibody.

questions.text: Which of the following criteria favors immunogenicity of a substance?
questions.explanation: Larger, chemically complex foreign molecules tend to be more immunogenic because they offer more distinct epitopes and peptides for presentation. Small simple molecules and resistance to processing do not favor a conventional protein immune response.

questions.text: A previously healthy although unvaccinated 3 year old boy is diagnosed with epiglottitis due to Hemophilus influenza B. The capsular polysaccharides of this infectious agent is classified as a Thymic independent antigen. In stimulating the immune response it will
questions.explanation: Unconjugated polysaccharides can trigger mature B cells without conventional peptide-specific helper T cells.

questions.text: Which of the following characterise the heterophil antigens
options: They are antigen with similar epitope
Can cause a lot of clinical syndromes like rheumatic fever
Their antibodies react with their shared epitopes
questions.explanation: Cross-reactive antigenic determinants explain shared antibody binding and poststreptococcal molecular mimicry.

questions.text: Which of the following increase the antigenicity except
options: Protein is more antigenic than lipid
The intradermal injection route is more antigenic than intravascular
High level of the antigen can cause a lot of activation to the immune system
The antigen molecular weight is important increase antigenicity
questions.explanation: Antigen dose is not monotonically immunogenic; very high doses can favor unresponsiveness, whereas composition, size and route influence response.

questions.text: Talk about the criteria of antigen
questions.modelAnswer: Define antigen as specifically recognized material and immunogen as material eliciting a response. Discuss foreignness, molecular size, chemical complexity, processability, dose, route, adjuvants and host factors. Protein antigens often recruit T help; unconjugated polysaccharides can stimulate B cells independently; haptens require carrier conjugation.
questions.explanation: Define antigen as specifically recognized material and immunogen as material eliciting a response. Discuss foreignness, molecular size, chemical complexity, processability, dose, route, adjuvants and host factors. Protein antigens often recruit T help; unconjugated polysaccharides can stimulate B cells independently; haptens require carrier conjugation.

questions.text: The smallest biochemical unit of an antigen that can bind to components of immune system is
questions.explanation: Epitope denotes the antigen determinant; paratope is the receptor site, hapten a carrier-dependent antigen, and isotype an antibody class.

questions.text: Large molecules are more immunogenic than small molecules as they:
questions.explanation: Larger antigens usually provide more epitopes, rather than a universal better receptor fit or depot effect.

questions.text: Regarding haptens, which one of the following is the MOST accurate?
options: A hapten is high molecular weight substance that is not immunogenic by itself but can react specifically with an antibody.
A hapten cannot induce antibody by itself but when covalently bound to a carrier protein can do so.
A hapten is defined by its ability to bind to the smaller of the two polypeptides that comprise the class I MHC proteins.
A hapten can bind to the antigen receptor of CD4-positive T cells without being processed by macrophages.
A hapten is the antigen-binding site in the hypervariable region of IgG.
questions.explanation: A hapten binds antibody but usually needs covalent linkage to a protein carrier to elicit a T-dependent antibody response.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE about superantigens?
options: They can only trigger CD8+ T cells
They are high molecular weight antigens that can trigger T cell proliferation in the absence of antigen presenting cells
They can activate all B lymphocytes by binding to IgM
They activate large numbers of T cells by directly binding to the TCRβ chain and class II MHC
questions.explanation: Superantigens bridge MHC II and the Vβ region of TCR outside conventional peptide-specific recognition, activating many T cells.

questions.text: A patient with tularemia was treated with streptomycin. After his symptoms have resolved he returned to the hospital with a raised itchy skin rash and fever. The drug was discontinued and his symptoms subsided. What was the role of streptomycin in this case?
options: It acted as a B cell mitogen
It acted as a provider of costimulatory signals
questions.explanation: A small drug molecule may become immunogenic after binding a host protein carrier.

questions.text: Which of the following substances will not stimulate an immune response unless they are bound to a larger molecule?
questions.explanation: Haptens need an immunogenic carrier for an antibody response; antibodies themselves can be antigenic without hapten behavior.

questions.text: Super antigens cause a burst of cytokines production by T cells due to their ability to cross link:
options: Variable β of TCR and MHC-II
questions.explanation: Superantigens bridge TCR Vβ with MHC-II outside conventional peptide recognition; CD3/CD8 or CD28 pairings do not explain it.

questions.text: Which one of the following sets of cells can present antigen to helper T cells?
options: B cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells are professional MHC II antigen-presenting cells for CD4 helper T cells.

questions.text: Which one of the following sets of cells can present antigen to helper T cells?
options: B cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells are professional MHC II antigen-presenting cells for CD4 helper T cells.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules present endogenously synthesized antigens?
questions.explanation: MHC class I ordinarily presents peptides generated from intracellular proteins to CD8 T cells. MHC class II presents peptides from endosomal processing to CD4 T cells.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules present extracellular antigens that are phagocytosed?
questions.explanation: Phagocytosed extracellular proteins enter endosomal processing and are ordinarily presented on MHC class II to CD4 T cells.

questions.text: Which of the following is a professional antigen-presenting cell that constitutively expresses both MHC class I and MHC class II antigens?
questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells and express MHC class II as well as MHC class I.

questions.text: Antigen presenting cells are required for T cell recognition of antigen. This task is achieved by presenting antigen in association with
questions.explanation: Conventional T cells recognize a peptide together with the MHC molecule displaying it; TCR is the lymphocyte receptor for that complex.

questions.text: Which of the following cell types lacks HLA antigens?
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack the normal MHC class I antigen-presentation machinery found in nucleated cells.

questions.text: Which of the following cells recognizes peptide fragments presented by class I MHC molecules
questions.explanation: CD8 is the coreceptor for MHC class I; conventional CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize peptides presented by class I molecules.

questions.text: Which of the following cells load peptide fragments into MHC class II molecules?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells process internalized proteins and load peptides onto MHC class II for presentation to helper T cells.

questions.text: T cell receptors, when co-expressed with CD8 molecules are restricted to recognizing and binding peptide fragments associated with
questions.explanation: CD8 binds MHC class I and stabilizes recognition of a peptide-MHC I complex by the T-cell receptor.

questions.text: T cell receptors, when co-expressed with CD4 molecules, are restricted to recognizing and binding peptide fragments associated with
questions.explanation: CD4 binds MHC class II, supporting the interaction of helper T cells with peptide-MHC II on antigen-presenting cells.

questions.text: In humans, MHC class II molecules are expressed by
options: B cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages
questions.explanation: B cells, dendritic cells and macrophages are the principal professional antigen-presenting populations with MHC class II expression.

questions.text: Regarding MHC proteins and the genes that encode them, which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
options: The genes encoding class II proteins are highly polymorphic. Whereas genes encoding class I proteins are not.
The genes encoding class I MHC proteins are located on a different chromosome from the genes encoding class II MHC proteins.
The genes are codominant, and each person expresses class I and class II genes inherited from both mother and father.
Class II MHC proteins are found on the surface of all cells, whereas class IT MHC proteins are found only on the surface of phagocytes.
questions.explanation: HLA alleles are expressed codominantly: products inherited from both parents contribute to an individual’s antigen-presentation repertoire.

questions.text: As an immune evasion mechanism HSV 1 and 2 depress the expression of MHC class I molecules on the surface of infected cells. Which co-receptor‘s binding would be inhibited by this technique?
questions.explanation: CD8 binds MHC I as a T-cell coreceptor.

questions.text: Major histocompatibility complex characterized by all of the following except
options: It's present in all types of cells
questions.explanation: MHC is inherited and polymorphic; mature erythrocytes do not display it, so all cell types is false.

questions.text: Which of the following chromosome express MHC protein
questions.explanation: The major HLA locus is chromosome 6; β2-microglobulin is a separate chromosome-15 gene, not offered.

questions.text: Which of the following genes express MHC class 1
questions.explanation: HLA-A encodes classical MHC-I; DP, DQ and DR encode II.

questions.text: Which of the following contain MHC proteins
questions.explanation: Trophoblast expresses nonclassical HLA such as HLA-G, unlike the conventional mature RBC/gamete exclusions; class of MHC should be specified.

questions.text: Which of the following cells contain only MHC-1
questions.explanation: Resting hepatocytes mainly express MHC-I; macrophages/DC/B cells are professional MHC-II APCs.

questions.text: talk about importance of MHC protein
questions.modelAnswer: MHC I presents predominantly intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells, permitting recognition of infected or abnormal host cells. MHC II presents predominantly vesicular/extracellular peptides to CD4 T cells, supporting macrophage activation and B-cell help. MHC polymorphism broadens population peptide recognition, shapes disease susceptibility and is central to tissue-transplant compatibility; selected nonclassical MHC molecules also regulate NK cells.
points: MHC I presents predominantly intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells, permitting recognition of infected or abnormal host cells.
MHC II presents predominantly vesicular/extracellular peptides to CD4 T cells, supporting macrophage activation and B-cell help.

questions.text: Which of the following is CORRECT regarding MHCI?
options: It generates peptides, complexes them for presentation to helper T cells
It presents antigens from the extracellular environment
It generates peptides, complexes them for presentation to NK cells
It presents antigens that are present in the cytosol
It activates T lymphocytes by binding to CD3 molecule
questions.explanation: MHC-I displays cytosol-derived peptides to CD8 cells; it does not itself generate peptides or bind CD3 as a ligand.

questions.text: Class I major histocompatibility complex (MHC-I):
options: Expressed on all cells of the body
Is encoded for on the short arm of chromosome 16
Has a low level of polymorphism
Encoded by HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-C
questions.explanation: Classical MHC-I genes are HLA-A, B and C; their heavy-chain locus is chromosome 6, not 16, and mature RBCs lack MHC.

questions.text: Which of the following polypeptide is important for the expression of MHC I on the cell membrane?
questions.explanation: β2-microglobulin stabilizes the MHC-I heavy chain for surface expression; cytokines are regulatory signals.

questions.text: The part of processed antigen that binds to the MHC molecule and recognized by T-cells?
questions.explanation: The antigenic determinant is an epitope; paratope is the receptor binding site and chaperones aid folding.

questions.text: Which of the following cell surfaces does not have Major Histocompatibility complex?
questions.explanation: Mature erythrocytes lack MHC; leukocytes and T cells are nucleated and express MHC-I.

subjects.name: Microbiology
subjects.lectures: Cytotoxic mechanisms, Helper T cells and cytokines, Superantigen activation, T-cell activation and regulation, T-cell development and selection, TCR recognition and signaling

questions.text: Fas/FasL interaction between target cell and T cytotoxic cell results in
options: Differentiation of T cytotoxic cells into effector killer cells
T cytotoxic cell secretion of IL-2
questions.explanation: Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell engages Fas on the target, activating caspases and inducing target-cell apoptosis.

questions.text: Which immunological process is affected in a person with a genetic defect in perforins and granzymes?
options: Defective killing of virally infected cells and malignant cells
questions.explanation: Perforin and granzymes mediate granule-dependent killing by cytotoxic lymphocytes, including destruction of infected and malignant target cells.

questions.text: When an activated CD8+ T cell encounters its appropriate peptide-MHC I complex on an infected cell, the next event is:
options: B cell receptors become cross linked and signaling ensues
CD8+ T cells destroy the infected cell
THO cells differentiate into TH2 cells
questions.explanation: An activated CD8 T cell recognizes its specific peptide-MHC I on an infected target and induces target-cell death.

questions.text: Upon encountering an appropriate peptide/MHC I on virally infected host cell
options: TH0 cells differentiate into TH2 cells
questions.explanation: Cognate MHC I recognition triggers CTL granule release into the target.

questions.text: Which of the following cells have the ability to produce perforin and granulozyme
questions.explanation: CTLs and NK cells use perforin and granzymes; B cells principally generate antibodies.

questions.text: compare between the Fas/Fasl pathway and perforin pathway
questions.modelAnswer: Perforin/granzyme killing uses calcium-dependent release of cytotoxic granules; perforin facilitates granzyme entry and granzymes activate target-cell apoptosis. The Fas/FasL pathway instead uses membrane Fas ligand on the effector to engage target Fas, activating death-receptor caspase signalling without a requirement for granule-mediated perforin delivery. Both produce apoptosis and allow precise target-cell killing.

questions.text: Cytotoxic T cells which kill their targets
options: Act via perforin and granzyme B
Recognise glycolipids in the context of MHC class-I molecules
questions.explanation: CD8 cytotoxic cells use perforin and granzyme; conventional TCR recognizes peptides, and IL-4/5 belong to type 2 immunity.

questions.text: Which molecules produced by CTL are directly involved in killing target cells
questions.explanation: Perforin and granzymes are CTL cytotoxic granule molecules; lactoferrin/lysozyme and complement fragments have other functions.

questions.text: Helper T cells are distinguished from cytotoxic T cells by the presence of...
questions.explanation: CD4 characterises the conventional helper T-cell lineage and binds MHC II; cytotoxic CD8 cells use CD8/MHC I.

questions.text: If early events of antigen recognition are dominated by IFN-γ, the result is:
options: TH-1 lymphocyte will be the dominant phenotype
TH-2 lymphocyte will be the dominant phenotype
Isotype switching of B-lymphocytes to IgE
Isotype switching of B-lymphocytes to IgA
questions.explanation: Early IFN-γ favors Th1 differentiation and a cell-mediated response; IL-4 instead favors Th2 development.

questions.text: Naive helper T cells (Th0) differentiate into Th1 when ______ from macrophages or ______ from NK cells is present.
questions.explanation: Macrophage IL-12 and early NK-cell IFN-γ promote differentiation toward Th1 immunity.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines are secreted by Th2 cells?
questions.explanation: IL-4 is a characteristic Th2 cytokine that reinforces Th2 differentiation and supports IgE class switching.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is not released by T helper 2 cells
questions.explanation: IFN-γ characterizes Th1 responses. IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 are associated with Th2 function, with IL-10 included in the historical Th2 profile.

questions.text: Regarding Th1 and Th2 cells, which one of the following statements is MOST accurate?
options: Th1 cells produce IFN-γ and promote cell-mediated immunity
Th2 cells produce IL-12 and enhance the formation of Th1 cells
TH1 produce IL-4 , IL-5 and IL-13 and promote humoral immunity
Th2 cells produce IFN-γ and IL-2 and promote cell-mediated immunity
Both TH1 and TH2 have class II MHC proteins on their outer cell membranes
questions.explanation: Th1 IFN-γ promotes macrophage activation and cell-mediated immunity. IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 instead belong to the typical Th2 profile.

questions.text: If early events of immune response lead to strong innate immunity and predominant activated macrophages, what is the suspected T helper subset to predominate?
questions.explanation: The classical macrophage–IL-12–IFN-γ feedback loop favors Th1 differentiation and macrophage-mediated cellular defense.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is essential for macrophage activation?
questions.explanation: IFN-γ is the key cytokine for classical macrophage activation and enhanced killing of intracellular pathogens.

questions.text: A major source of IL-12 is...., and its immunological effect is....
options: Macrophage/ Differentiation of naive THO into TH1
B lymphocytes/ stimulation of humoral immune responses
Mast cells/ Release of inflammatory mediators
questions.explanation: Activated macrophages produce IL-12, which promotes Th1 differentiation and also activates NK cells.

questions.text: The cytokine profile consisting of IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10 and IL-13 is a feature of
questions.explanation: The combination of IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 identifies a Th2-associated cytokine profile, supporting humoral and anti-helminth responses.

questions.text: Which of the following is a well-known effect of interleukin-8?
options: Suppression of interleukin release by helper T cell.
Switch from IgM to IgG synthesis.
questions.explanation: CXCL8 (IL-8) is a chemokine that attracts and activates neutrophils at sites of infection or inflammation.

questions.text: Which of the following is a well-known effect of IL-12
options: Induction of Th1 differentiation from naive Th0 cells
Suppression of interleukin release by helper T cell.
Switch from IgM to IgG synthesis.
questions.explanation: IL-12 from antigen-presenting cells favors differentiation of naive helper T cells toward Th1 responses.

questions.text: Th2-associated cytokines counter-regulate which of the following?
questions.explanation: Th2-associated IL-10 and IL-4 counter classical macrophage/Th1 activity while supporting humoral responses.

questions.text: One of the cells involved in certain autoimmune diseases is described as CD3 Positive, CD4 positive. Regarding this cell, which one of the following is the most accurate regarding its function?
options: Recognizes antigen in association with class I MHC proteins
Presents antigen in association with class II MHC proteins
questions.explanation: CD3+CD4+ helper T cells can produce IL-2 after activation, supporting lymphocyte growth; their conventional antigen recognition uses MHC class II.

questions.text: Regarding TH1, TH2, and TH17, which one of the following is the most accurate?
options: TH17 cells produce IL-17 which stimulates the production of TH2 cells
The production of TH1 cells is enhanced by IL-4, whereas the production of TH2 cells is enhanced by IL-2
TH2 cells synthesize IFN-γ which is important in controlling infections caused by Staphylococcus aureus and other pyogenic bacteria
TH1 cells are involved in delayed hypersensitivity reactions as control of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Th2 cells are the most important cells in defense against tumor cells
questions.explanation: Th1 responses activate macrophages and underlie delayed hypersensitivity, including the cellular defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.text: Regarding cytokines, which one of the following is the MOST accurate?
options: IL-2 is made by B cells and increases class switching from IgM to IgG
IL-4 is made by cytotoxic T cells and mediates the killing of virus infected cells
IL-12 is made by eosinophils and enhances immediate hypersensitivity reactions
IFN-γ is made by Th1 cells and activates macrophages to phagocytose more effectively
IL-4 is made by TH1 cells and induce class switching from IgM to IgE
questions.explanation: Th1-derived IFN-γ enhances macrophage antimicrobial activity; IL-4 instead promotes Th2-associated responses and IgE switching.

questions.text: Regarding the function of chemokines, which of the following statements is MOST accurate?
options: Chemokines penetrate the membranes of target cells during attack by cytotoxic T cells
Chemokines bind to the T cell receptor outside of the antigen binding site and activate many T cells
Chemokines attract neutrophils to the site of bacterial infection, thereby playing a role in the inflammatory response
Chemokines induce gene switching in B cells, which increase amount of IgE, predisposing to allergy
Chemokines are produced TH2 cells inducing delayed hypersensitivity reactions
questions.explanation: Chemokines provide directional signals for leukocyte migration; CXCL8 recruits and activates neutrophils during bacterial inflammation.

questions.text: A CD4+ T cell exposed to IL-12 produced by antigen presenting cells in response to microbe- derived lipopolysaccharide. This CD4+ T cell will:
questions.explanation: IL-12 promotes Th1 differentiation, favoring macrophage activation and cell-mediated defense rather than an IL-4-dominant Th2 response.

questions.text: CD4+ T cells that respond to intracellular pathogens by recruiting and activating phagocytic cells are termed
questions.explanation: Th1 helper cells respond to intracellular microbes by producing cytokines, especially IFN-γ, that activate macrophage antimicrobial functions.

questions.text: Patients with HIV infection usually have a deviation towards a TH2 response early in the course of their disease, which of the following cytokines would be increased in a patient with a CD4 count of 500/mm3?
questions.explanation: Under the stem’s stipulated Th2 bias, IL-10 is the characteristic listed cytokine.

questions.text: 45 year old male patient with tuberculoid leprosy has skin granulomas with elevated amounts of IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-β. Which of the following immune cells is responsible for this cytokine pattern?
questions.explanation: Tuberculoid leprosy is associated with protective Th1 cellular immunity.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokine attract neutrophil and secreted from TH-17
questions.explanation: Th17-produced IL-17 promotes neutrophil recruitment mainly by inducing chemokines in tissue cells; IL-8 is the direct chemoattractant but not the signature listed Th17 product.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is used to differentiate effector T-cell to TH1
questions.explanation: IL-12 supports Th1 differentiation, unlike IL-2 growth or IL-6/TNF inflammatory roles.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is produced by CD4+ CD25+ T cells
questions.explanation: Regulatory T cells suppress using IL-10 and TGF-β; the other pairs emphasize growth, inflammation or antiviral defense.

questions.text: Regarding TH-1 & TH-2, which one of the following statements is correct
options: TH-2 produce IL-12 and promote formation of TH-1
TH-1 produce IL-17 that enhances neutrophils activity
TH-2 and TH-1 both positively regulate each other
questions.explanation: Th1 promotes macrophage-centered cellular immunity; Th2/Th1 do not simply reinforce each other, and Th17 makes IL-17.

questions.text: Which of the following belongs to INF γ?
options: It is produced by all nucleated cells of the body
questions.explanation: IFN-γ activates macrophages; type I IFNs come from infected nucleated cells, and neutrophil chemotaxis has other mediators.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT TRUE about TH1 cells?
questions.explanation: Th1 cells recognize peptide-MHC, not soluble intact antigen; they bear CD4 and IL-2 receptor and produce IFN-γ.

questions.text: Macrophage activation to kill intracellular pathogens is primarily mediated by
questions.explanation: IFN-γ activates macrophages for intracellular microbial killing; IL-2 primarily supports lymphocyte growth.

questions.text: An elderly man with diabetes develops a carbuncle on his back. He takes a topical antibiotic but quickly develops fever, hypotension and a desquamating skin rash. The toxin responsible for these symptoms is a
questions.explanation: Toxic shock syndrome can result from a superantigen that activates many T cells through Vβ-dependent binding, provoking systemic cytokine release.

questions.text: An elderly man with diabetes develops a carbuncle on his back. He takes a topical antibiotic but quickly develops fever, hypotension and a desquamating skin rash. How does the toxin responsible for these symptoms cause them?
options: It activates B-lymphocytes in a non-specific manner
It stimulates T-lymphocytes in a non-specific manner
questions.explanation: Superantigens cross-link MHC class II with selected TCR Vβ families, bypassing ordinary peptide-specific recognition and activating many T cells.

questions.text: Viral or bacterial proteins that cross-link a certain variable β domain of a T-cell receptor to class II MHC molecules, causing polyclonal stimulation of T cells, overproduction of cytokines and shock are:
questions.explanation: Superantigens bind outside the MHC class II peptide groove and engage TCR Vβ, inducing widespread T-cell activation and cytokine release.

questions.text: A 35 year old female using tampons during menstruation develops severe hypotension, desquamative skin rash and enters into a shock state. Culture of tampons reveals a Staphylococcus aureus strain. The doctor recommends an ELISA to detect TSST-1 production. The pathologic sequelae in this condition is due to release of:
options: Acute phase proteins( CRP and MBL)
Activation of alternative pathway of complement activation
questions.explanation: TSST-1 is a staphylococcal superantigen. Broad T-cell activation and inflammatory cytokine release drive fever, hypotension and systemic toxicity.

questions.text: A 35 year old female using tampons during menstruation develops severe hypotension, desquamative skin rash and enters into a shock state. Culture of tampons reveals a Staphylococcus aureus strain. Which T cells are selected for activation by TSST-1?
options: According to its T cell receptor specificity for the toxin (antigen)
T cells expressing a certain variable β chain in their TCRs
T cells expressing a variable a chain in their TCRs
T cells expressing γδ chains in their TCRs
T cells expressing CD4 and CD25
questions.explanation: Superantigen responsiveness depends mainly on the TCR Vβ family rather than ordinary peptide-specific receptor recognition.

questions.text: Which of the following are superantigens?
questions.explanation: TSST-1 is a staphylococcal superantigen that links MHC class II to selected TCR Vβ regions, causing broad cytokine release.

questions.text: A 35 year old female using tampons during menstruation develops severe hypotension, desquamative skin rash and enters into a shock state. Culture of tampons reveals a Staphylococcus aureus strain. The doctor recommends an ELISA to detect TSST-1 production. If the toxin is positive in this case so it acts as a.......
questions.explanation: TSST-1 belongs to the superantigen class that activates many T cells.

questions.text: A diabetic patient developed a blister on the heal of his foot .Culture results reveal Staph aureus and although he was treated with topical antibiotics, he developed fever and hypotension and desquamating skin rash. How does the toxin responsible for his symptoms cause these signs
options: It acts as an IL-1 homologue
It-cross links MHC class II molecules to TCRs polyclonally
questions.explanation: Staphylococcal superantigens bridge MHC II and TCR V-beta, activating many T cells.

questions.text: Which of the following costimulatary molecules are needed for T-helper cell activation?
options: MHC class I interacting with T cell receptor
questions.explanation: B7 on an APC binds CD28 on the naive T cell to deliver classical co-stimulation.

questions.text: Which one of the following is TRUE regarding T cell activation and signaling?
options: Binding of B7 molecule to CTLA-4 promotes an inhibitory response
MHC II molecule binds to the CD8 coreceptor to initiate activation
In the absence of costimulation, the T cell produces TNF-α
The essential cytokine released following activation is IL-1
Binding of CD40 on the APC with CD28 on the T cell is essential for activation
questions.explanation: CTLA-4 competes for B7 and delivers an inhibitory signal, limiting activated T-cell proliferation.

questions.text: If tumor cells isolated from a solid tumor were transfected to express costimulatory molecules, which of the following molecules would be the best candidate to achieve this goal?
questions.explanation: B7 molecules on an antigen-presenting surface engage CD28 on T cells to provide costimulation. CD28 and CTLA-4 are T-cell receptors.

questions.text: A molecule that appears on activated T cells essential for switching off an immune response is
questions.explanation: CTLA-4 is induced on activated T cells and binds B7 more avidly than CD28, limiting further activation and proliferation.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cell surface protein induced on activated T cells with a higher affinity for B7 molecules on antigen presenting cells than CD28 AND what is its effect?
questions.explanation: CTLA-4 binds B7 with higher avidity than CD28 and delivers inhibitory signaling, helping limit activated T-cell responses.

questions.text: T cells stimulated by peptide/MHC complexes in absence of costimulation enter into
questions.explanation: Antigen recognition without adequate costimulation can render a naive T cell anergic rather than productively activated.

questions.text: Cell mediated immunity is conducted by:
options: B cells, NK and cytotoxic T cells
B cells, NK and T helper cells
Activated macrophages, T helper and T cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Cell-mediated adaptive immunity uses T cells and activated macrophages. Antibody-dependent mechanisms are conventionally grouped with humoral immunity.

questions.text: Regulatory T-cells secrete which of the following cytokines:
questions.explanation: Regulatory T cells can produce both IL-10 and TGF-β to suppress immune responses; the combined answer is the most complete. IL-1 and IL-6 principally support inflammatory responses.

questions.text: Memory T cells differ from naive T cells by:
options: Naive T cells need a smaller amount of antigen to be activated than that needed by memory cells and produce less amounts of cytokines
Memory T cells are activated by less amounts of antigen than naive T cells and produce much more cytokines
Naive T cells don’t need costimulation while memory T cells do
Memory T cells give the same response as naive T cells but need less costimulation
Memory cells give a rapid response that wanes quickly while naive cells give a slower response that continues for long periods of time
questions.explanation: Memory T cells respond more sensitively and rapidly to antigen and can produce effector cytokines more vigorously than naive cells.

questions.text: Which one of the following sets can present antigen to TH cells
options: B cells and cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: B cells and dendritic cells both process antigen and present peptides on MHC class II to helper T cells.

questions.text: As regards function of cell mediated immunity , which of the following is CORRECT
options: Activation of classical pathway of complement activation
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells eliminate virally infected host cells. Toxin neutralization, antibody opsonization and antibody-triggered complement are humoral mechanisms.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines induces activation of T cells and hence called T cell growth factor?
questions.explanation: IL-2 produced by activated T cells drives their proliferation and differentiation, explaining its traditional name T-cell growth factor.

questions.text: Which of the following cells require interaction with both peptide/MHC and a set of costimulatory second signals from an antigen presenting cell to become activated?
questions.explanation: Naive T cells require both cognate peptide-MHC recognition and costimulation from an activated antigen-presenting cell for productive priming.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules competes with CD28 for binding of B7 on antigen presenting cells?
questions.explanation: CTLA-4 and CD28 both bind B7, but CTLA-4 delivers an inhibitory signal and binds more avidly.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is used for proliferation of T cell
questions.explanation: IL-2 drives activated T-cell proliferation; IL-1/6/TNF serve prominent inflammatory roles.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about co-stimulatory molecule of Tc
options: CD28 of Tc binds to B7 of nucleated cell
CD40L of T-cytotoxic binds to CD40 of nucleated cell
ICAM-1 of nucleated cell binds to LFA-1 of Tc
questions.explanation: B7 on APCs binds CD28 on CD8 T cells during priming; ICAM/LFA1 mainly stabilizes adhesion and CD40 is not a CD28 ligand.

questions.text: What happens if T cell lacks co-stimulatory molecules
options: The T cell becomes in state of anergy
The T cell can't bind to non-self antigen on MHC
The T cell can't transduce 1ry signal
T cell can't stabilise the TCR to antigen in MHC
questions.explanation: Recognition without adequate costimulation leads to anergy/nonresponse; the TCR can still bind peptide-MHC and transmit initial signals.

questions.text: Which of the following is inhibitory mechanism used to suppress immune response
options: CTLA-4 which inhibits T cell by binding to B7 after T cell stimulation
PD protein that expresses on T cell
T-regulatory cell that secretes cytokines that inhibit immune response
All of the following are true
questions.explanation: CTLA4, PD1 and regulatory T-cell suppression all restrain immune activation.

questions.text: Which of the following interactions is required for the activation of T helpers
questions.explanation: B7-CD28 supplies activating costimulation; helper TCR uses MHC-II, LFA1 binds ICAM, and CTLA4 is inhibitory.

questions.text: Why is clonal expansion so important?
options: To increase the numbers of specific cells
questions.explanation: Clonal expansion increases antigen-specific cell number; target killing and secretion are later effector actions.

questions.text: Costimulatory molecules help T cell responses by
options: Degrading antigen so it can bind in the MHC groove
Increasing T cell activation via sending 2nd activation signal
Binding to MHC molecules containing immunogenic peptides
questions.explanation: Costimulation provides a second activating signal; processing and MHC binding are distinct functions.

questions.text: Activation of naive T lymphocytes is best achieved by which antigen presenting cells?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the most effective primers of naive T cells; neutrophils and mast cells are not standard professional primers.

questions.text: Cytokine primarily involved in T cell proliferation and development is
questions.explanation: IL-2 drives activated T-cell proliferation; IL-12 directs Th1 differentiation. Printed key a correctly selects IL-2.

questions.text: Down regulation of CMI is mediated by expression of ______ on T lymphocytes
questions.explanation: CTLA-4 restrains T-cell activation by binding B7; CD40L activates APC/B-cell interactions and PD-L1 is the ligand of PD-1.

questions.text: 2ry immune response differs from 1ry immune response in:
options: Memory cells secrete different types of cytokines
Memory cells give stronger and faster response
2ry response is mediated by naive cells
questions.explanation: Memory populations generate faster, stronger responses and generally have lower costimulatory requirements.

questions.text: Positive selection of thymocytes during their development in the thymus is critical for
questions.explanation: Positive selection retains thymocytes able to recognize self MHC, establishing MHC restriction of the mature T-cell repertoire.

questions.text: An education process of T-lymphocytes that ensures that only T cells capable of recognizing antigens in association of self MHC molecules survive is called
questions.explanation: Thymocytes that appropriately recognize self peptide-MHC receive survival signals during positive selection. Strongly self-reactive cells instead undergo negative selection.

questions.text: The major aim of Negative Selection process during development of immature thymocytes in the thymus is
options: Maturation of professional antigen presenting cells
questions.explanation: Negative selection removes developing T cells with potentially harmful strong self-reactivity, helping establish central tolerance.

questions.text: Regarding events that occur in the thymus during maturation of T cells, which one of the following is the most accurate?
options: Most mature T cells have both CD4 and CD8 proteins in their surface to ensure their ability to react with antigen presented by MHC class I or II proteins
T cells bearing antigen receptors that react strongly with self-peptide–MHC complexes can be deleted by negative selection
Superantigens are “super” because they play a selective role in both the positive and negative selection that occurs in the thymus
T cells bearing antigen receptors that recognize antigen in association with foreign MHC proteins survive, a process known as positive selection
T cells bearing antigen receptors reacting with self MHC proteins are deleted by a process called negative selection
questions.explanation: Negative selection deletes developing T cells with harmful strong self-reactivity; positive selection preserves useful self-MHC recognition.

questions.text: Positive selection refers to
options: The ability of single positive cells to bind both MHC class I and II
Acquisition of TCR by developing thymocytes
Migration of stem cells to the thymus to become T cells
Programmed cell death of single positive T cells
Recognition of MHC by double positive (CD4+, CD8+) thymocytes
questions.explanation: Positive selection tests whether double-positive thymocytes recognize self MHC.

questions.text: Which of the following is true about maturation of T cell
questions.explanation: T-cell maturation occurs in thymus with positive self-MHC and negative self-antigen selection.

questions.text: The basic structure of a T cell receptor consists of:
options: covalently linked CD3 and CD20 molecules.
a membrane-bound αβ or γδ heterodimer.
a complex of disulfide-linked heavy and light chains.
questions.explanation: TCR is a membrane-bound disulfide-linked αβ or γδ heterodimer; associated CD3 provides signalling.

questions.text: Initiation of an intracellular signal after binding of an antigen to a TCR on T lymphocytes is mediated through:
questions.explanation: CD3 and ζ chains carry signaling motifs associated with the TCR; antigen recognition by TCR is transmitted through these accessory chains.

questions.text: Stabilization of interaction between a T helper cell and MHC class II on APCs is achieved by:
questions.explanation: CD4 binds an invariant region of MHC class II and supports helper T-cell recognition of the peptide-MHC complex.

questions.text: CD3 molecules on T cells act as a:
questions.explanation: CD3 is the signal-transducing accessory complex of the T-cell receptor; the TCR variable chains perform antigen recognition.

questions.text: The importance of the CD4 molecule on T cells is:
options: Stabilization of interaction of APCs with TH cells
questions.explanation: CD4 binds MHC class II and supports helper T-cell contact with antigen-presenting cells. CD3 is the principal TCR-associated signaling complex.

questions.text: One of the cells involved in certain autoimmune diseases is described as CD3 positive, CD8 positive. Regarding this cell, which one of the following is the most accurate regarding its function?
options: Recognizes antigen in association with class I MHC proteins
Presents antigen in association with class II MHC proteins
questions.explanation: Conventional CD8 T cells recognize antigenic peptides on MHC class I, allowing recognition of infected or abnormal host cells.
