Case context: A 35 year old female using tampons during menstruation develops severe hypotension, desquamative skin rash and enters into a shock state. Culture of tampons reveals a Staphylococcus aureus strain. The doctor recommends an ELISA to detect TSST-1 production. If the toxin is positive in this case so it acts as a.......

For this case, what is the mechanism of action of the toxin?
options: Binds to its receptor on endothelial blood vessels inducing vasodilation and increasing vascular permeability
Activates alternative pathway of complement activation inducing C3a and C5a anaphylatoxins)
Acts on mast cells and basophils releasing histamine and other vasoactive mediators
Cross links variable β domain of TCR on T cells and class II MHC molecules on APCs resulting in polyclonal stimulation of T cells and outpouring of proinflammatory cytokines
Cross links BCRs on B lymphocytes leading to excessive production of immunoglobulins
questions.explanation: Superantigens bind MHC II and TCR V-beta outside the conventional peptide recognition site.

questions.text: T-helper cell recognize Ag by ______
options: TCR attachment to MHC-I and stabilized by CD8
TCR attaches to Ag presented by MHC-II and stabilized by CD4
questions.explanation: CD4 TCR recognizes peptide-MHC-II; CD8 stabilizes MHC-I recognition and nonspecific recognition does not describe helper TCR.

questions.text: Which of the following is function of CD3
options: Stabilise the attachment to MHC protein
It is secretory protein to fight bacteria
questions.explanation: CD3 carries signaling ITAMs; CD4/CD8 are coreceptors and B7-CD28 provide costimulation.

questions.text: Which of the following cells recognize peptides associated with MHC-I molecule
questions.explanation: CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize peptide-MHC-I; CD4 helpers recognize MHC-II and B cells native antigen.

questions.text: The basic structure of a T cell receptor consists of:
options: A complex of disulfide-linked heavy and light chains
Covalently linked CD3 and CD20 molecules
questions.explanation: Conventional TCR is a membrane αβ heterodimer, not immunoglobulin heavy/light chains, CD3-CD20 or peptide-MHC.

questions.text: T cells recognise antigen
options: When presented on the surface of antigen presenting cells
Following presentation by pattern recognition receptors
questions.explanation: Conventional T cells recognize antigen as surface peptide-MHC complexes, not soluble intact antigen or PRR presentation.

questions.text: CD4 T cells are generally restricted by:
questions.explanation: CD4 binds MHC-II; CD8 binds MHC-I and β2-microglobulin is an MHC-I subunit.

questions.text: MHC class I molecules are primarily involved in
questions.explanation: MHC-I presents intracellular peptides to antiviral cytotoxic CD8 cells; it does not specialize in glycolipids or neutrophil activation.

questions.text: The cell which receives antigen presented by MHC-I molecule is
questions.explanation: MHC-I presents peptide to CD8 T cells; CD4 recognizes MHC-II and B cells bind native antigen.

subjects.name: Microbiology
subjects.lectures: Antibody effector functions, Antibody structure and specificity, B-cell activation and T-cell help, B-cell receptors and differentiation, Class switching and affinity maturation, Immunoglobulin classes and functions, Primary and secondary responses

questions.text: Choose the CORRECT sentence regarding antibody-dependent cell cytotoxicity (ADCC)?
options: It is carried out by B cells only.
It's the main mechanism for killing intracellular microbes.
It's mostly mediated by IgM antibody.
It involves Fc receptors on the effector cells.
questions.explanation: ADCC occurs when an effector cell uses Fc receptors to bind antibody coating a target and then kills that target.

questions.text: Which biological function of an immunoglobulin molecule can prevent a toxin from reaching its specific target cell?
questions.explanation: Neutralizing antibody binds a toxin and blocks its interaction with the target cell.

questions.text: Opsonization function of IgG is mediated by
questions.explanation: Antigen-bound IgG engages phagocyte Fcγ receptors through its heavy-chain constant Fc region, promoting uptake.

questions.text: A process of coating particulate antigen with IgG or and complement component C3b to enhance phagocytosis and killing activity of phagocytic cells is called
questions.explanation: Opsonization coats a particle with antibody or complement to enhance phagocyte recognition and ingestion.

questions.text: All of the following cells mediate ADCC (Antibody dependent cellular cytotoxicity) EXCEPT
questions.explanation: NK cells and several phagocyte/granulocyte populations mediate antibody-dependent cytotoxicity; mast cells are principally IgE-triggered mediator-releasing cells in this conventional classification.

questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins is MOST efficient at complement activation
questions.explanation: Pentameric antigen-bound IgM is highly efficient at recruiting C1q and initiating the classical complement pathway.

questions.text: IgM is the most efficient at:
questions.explanation: IgM pentamers efficiently activate classical complement through antigen-associated C1q binding.

questions.text: The process by which IgG and/or C3b enhance phagocytosis is called:
questions.explanation: IgG Fc and deposited C3b enhance phagocyte uptake, which is opsonization; neutralization, cytolysis and clumping are distinct effects.

questions.text: The binding of antibodies to microbial epitopes or soluble molecules in a manner that inhibits the ability of these microbes to bind to host cell surfaces is termed
questions.explanation: Neutralization blocks receptor engagement by toxin or microbe; opsonization enhances uptake, agglutination clumps particles and precipitation aggregates soluble antigen.

questions.text: Immunoglobulins can tag antigens for destruction and removal by effector cells. This process is termed
questions.explanation: Tagging a target for effector uptake/removal is opsonization; ADCC specifically kills antibody-coated cells and is a narrower outcome.

questions.text: A 71 year old female patient develops fever and inflammation of her left knee 3 days after discharge from the hospital following knee replacement surgery. Staph epidermidis organisms causing infection are initially not targets of the patient’s phagocytic cells. However after IgG1 antibodies bind to their capsules, many Staph epidermidis cells are destroyed by phagocytosis. This process is known as:
questions.explanation: IgG coating enhances phagocyte uptake through Fc receptors.

questions.text: A person developed extracellular bacterial infection, and produced IgM in response, which of the following is the most important protective function of IgM?
questions.explanation: IgM efficiently activates complement; it is not a direct Fc-mediated opsonin and IgA dominates mucosal secretions.

questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins have binding site for C1q?
questions.explanation: IgM and appropriate IgG subclasses activate classical complement through C1q; IgD, IgA and IgE do not characteristically do so.

questions.text: Biological function of antibody is mediated by:
questions.explanation: Fc drives antibody effector functions; Fab/hypervariable domains bind antigen.

questions.text: Which one of the following antibodies is the most efficient in complement activation
questions.explanation: Pentameric IgM is especially efficient at classical complement activation; IgG subclasses vary and IgA/IgD/IgE are not main activators.

questions.text: Which of the following is TRUE regarding the Fab portion of immunoglobulin?
options: Mediates biological effector functions of Ab molecules (e.g. complement fixation).
Contains the idiotype of the Ig
Not important to binding of antigen.
questions.explanation: Fab includes variable regions and the antigen-binding site, carrying idiotypic determinants; Fc mediates the major effector interactions.

questions.text: The portion of the antigen that fits into the idiotype of an antibody or antigen receptor (BCR or TCR) is called
questions.explanation: An epitope is the antigenic determinant recognised by antibody or an antigen receptor; paratope denotes the receptor binding surface.

questions.text: The idiotype of an antibody refers to
options: Hypervariable regions of both heavy and light chains
questions.explanation: Idiotypic determinants reside in antibody variable regions, including contributions from heavy and light chains.

questions.text: If an individual was genetically unable to make J chains. Which immunoglobulin would be affected?
questions.explanation: J chain participates in polymeric IgM and dimeric secretory IgA assembly, rather than monomeric IgG.

questions.text: Idiotypic determinants are located within:
options: Hypervariable regions of heavy and light chains
questions.explanation: Idiotypic determinants arise from the antigen-binding variable regions of both heavy and light chains.

questions.text: Which one of the following properties of antibody is not dependent on the structure of the heavy-chain constant region:
options: Binding Fc receptors on phagocytic cells
questions.explanation: Antigen affinity is conferred by the variable binding site, while the heavy constant region governs class and effector interactions.

questions.text: Regarding the genes that encode antibodies, hypervariable regions are encoded by the genes of:
questions.explanation: The antigen-binding hypervariable regions are encoded in the variable domains of both immunoglobulin heavy and light chain genes.

questions.text: Which of the following statements describes Monoclonal antibodies
options: Antibodies sharing isotopes from different species
Antibodies against a single epitope and produced from a single clone of immortal cells
Antibodies with different affinities for the same antigen that induced them
Produced by fusion of a normal plasma cell with a B cell producing antibodies against a single epitope
Induced in the lab by B lymphocyte activation by endotoxin
questions.explanation: A monoclonal antibody population has one clone/specificity; classical hybridoma production fuses an antibody-producing lymphocyte with immortal myeloma, not two ordinary B cells.

questions.text: The constant region of the five major types of heavy chains of immunoglobulin molecules determines the molecule’s
questions.explanation: Heavy-chain constant domains determine isotype and effector activity; epitope is antigen, variable domains bind it, and ITAMs occur in signaling subunits.

questions.text: A term that describes the three dimensional shape of the antigen binding site of an antibody is the
questions.explanation: Idiotype describes variable-region antigenic determinants associated with the antibody binding specificity; isotype is class, allotype inherited variation, affinity/avidity binding strengths.

questions.text: Which of the following has a three-dimensional structure complementary to the idiotype of the antibody?
questions.explanation: The antigen epitope has a complementary shape to the antibody binding site; paratope denotes the antibody site itself and adjuvant enhances immunization.

questions.text: All of the following are true about the constant region of heavy chain except
options: It is responsible for the formation of the Fc portion of antibody
It is responsible for classification of antibody into 5 isotypes
It is responsible for complement activation in some Ig
It is responsible for specificity of the immunoglobulin
questions.explanation: Specificity is established by heavy/light variable domains; heavy constant region establishes Fc/isotype and effector functions.

questions.text: Which of the following is false about monoclonal antibody
options: It was secreted from one clone of B cell
It's formed by fusion of 2 cells myeloma and B cell
It is used for many therapeutic uses as tumor or vaccine
The life span of B-cell outside the body is long
questions.explanation: Ordinary B cells have limited culture longevity; hybridoma fusion combines antibody specificity with myeloma growth capacity.

questions.text: The specificity of an antibody is due to its?
questions.explanation: Antigen specificity lies in heavy/light hypervariable loops; valency and Fc describe binding count and effector function.

questions.text: Which of the following is an Ag binding site?
options: Constant region of both heavy and light chain
Variable region of both heavy and light chain
questions.explanation: Both heavy and light variable domains jointly form the antibody antigen-binding site.

questions.text: If early antigen recognition elicits IL-4, IL-5, IL-6 and IL-13, which of the following best describes the characteristic humoral outcome?
questions.explanation: The Th2-associated cytokine pattern promotes B-cell activation and immunoglobulin production rather than a classical Th1 delayed-hypersensitivity response.

questions.text: CD40 L on a T cell interacting with CD40 on B cell is important for:
options: Inhibition of immunoglobulin synthesis by B cells
Signal transduction of B cell receptor after binding to its specific epitope
Isotype class switching of IgM to IgG in a secondary immune response
Clonal selection of a certain B lymphocyte with a certain B cell receptor
questions.explanation: CD40L on helper T cells engages B-cell CD40 to support T-dependent class switching and maturation.

questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding Thymic Independent Antigens
options: Univalent antigens ( have one epitope only)
Need activation signals from T helper cells
Multivalent polysaccharide antigens with repeated epitopes
questions.explanation: Repeated epitopes on multivalent polysaccharides support T-independent B-cell activation without classical peptide-specific T-cell help.

questions.text: Follicular dendritic cells serve to:
options: Process antigen and present it to T-lymphocytes
Process antigen and present it to B-lymphocytes
Display antigen to T and B lymphocytes
questions.explanation: FDCs display retained native/immune-complex antigen to B cells rather than processing peptide for conventional T-cell presentation.

questions.text: Which of the following processes require T follicular helper cells :
options: Activation of B-lymphocytes in the early phase of humoral immune response
Recognition of antigen by a naive B-lymphocyte in primary follicles
Isotype switching and affinity maturation of B cells in humoral immune response
Clonal selection of a certain naive B lymphocyte specific for a certain epitope
Production of IgM antibodies against capsulated bacteria
questions.explanation: Follicular helper support drives germinal-center switching and affinity selection; initial antigen recognition/clonal specificity and T-independent IgM do not require Tfh.

questions.text: Which of the following induces secondary signals augmenting antigen recognition signals of BCR complex and important for B cell activation
options: Complement component (C3d) acting on complement receptor 2 on B lymphocytes
CTLA-4 on activated T helper cells
PAMPs on microbes acting on Toll like receptors on B-lymphocytes
questions.explanation: C3d-CR2 co-receptor engagement and microbial TLR ligands can augment BCR signals; CTLA4 provides T-cell inhibition, so a and c combine.

questions.text: An important feature of Thymic independent antigens is:
options: They are composed of a hapten conjugated to a carrier protein
They have repeated epitopes that cross link membrane bound immunoglobulins on B cells
They elicit a memory response on re-exposure to them
They lead to secretion of all isotypes of antibodies
Ubiquitous antigens in the body displayed on MHC molecules for T cells during their development
questions.explanation: Repetitive epitopes on TI-2 antigens crosslink BCRs; carrier proteins recruit T help, and strong switched memory is not the typical TI response.

questions.text: Which of the following is a Thymic dependent antigen?
questions.explanation: Streptococcal M protein is a T-dependent protein antigen; naked polysaccharide/LPS are TI and free penicillin is a hapten.

questions.text: Which of the following is characteristic of Thymic independent antigens?
options: Need activation signals from TH1 cells
Need activation signals from TH2 cells
questions.explanation: Repeating multivalent epitopes enable strong BCR crosslinking characteristic of TI-2 responses; Th1/Th2 help and classical memory are not required.

questions.text: Which one of the following is most likely to induce an IgM antibody response without the participation of helper T cells?
options: Pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide conjugated to diphtheria toxoid
questions.explanation: Unconjugated pneumococcal polysaccharide elicits TI IgM; protein toxoids and conjugated polysaccharide recruit T-cell help and TSST activates T cells.

questions.text: Activation of B cell occurs in
questions.explanation: Antigen-dependent B activation occurs in secondary lymphoid tissue such as lymph nodes; marrow/thymus are primary maturation sites.

questions.text: Thymic dependent activation includes all of the following except
options: The B cell acts as APC for T-helper cell
The B cell internalises the Ag by receptor mediated endocytosis
The B cell recognizes polysaccharide antigen
The B cell produces memory in thymic dependent
questions.explanation: Unconjugated polysaccharides typically induce T-independent responses; T-dependent proteins undergo uptake, presentation and memory differentiation.

questions.text: Which of the following immune components are most effective at destroying extracellular pathogens
questions.explanation: Antibodies from B cells neutralize and opsonize extracellular pathogens; T helper and interferon responses target different tasks.

questions.text: B lymphocytes once activated by thymus independent Ag, they differentiate into:
questions.explanation: Classical thymus-independent responses chiefly yield antibody-secreting cells and poor memory compared with T-dependent responses.

questions.text: Thymus dependent Ag in comparison with thymus independent Ag:
options: Produce only one isotype of ABs
Receives class switch signal via CD40-CD40L interaction
questions.explanation: T-dependent protein responses receive CD40L help and switch isotype; they produce memory and multiple isotypes.

questions.text: The best marker for identification of B lymphocyte is
questions.explanation: CD19 is a characteristic B-lineage surface marker and signaling coreceptor; CD3, CD4 and CD8 are principally T-cell markers.

questions.text: A plasma cell has developed from a B cell. Compared to the cell from which it was derived the plasma cell
options: Is a more efficient antigen-presenting cell
questions.explanation: Plasma cells specialize in secretion of soluble antibodies with the antigen specificity of their B-cell precursor.

questions.text: Which of the following biological effects is not an effect of IgG?
questions.explanation: Naive mature B cells characteristically express IgM and IgD, whereas class-switched B cells can express IgG.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is correct regarding TCR and BCR
options: BCR recognizes only processed protein antigens while TCR can recognize varieties of different antigen types
BCR is composed of an alpha polypeptide chain non covalently linked to a p2 microglobulin while TCR is composed of « and B chains
BCR is composed of membrane bound monomeric IgM and IgD antibodies while TCR is composed of two chains ( a and B )
TCR can react with two epitopes at a time while BCR can react only with one antigenic determinant at a time
The signal transducing molecule of TCR is CD3 while the signal transducing molecule of BCR is CD14
questions.explanation: Naive B cells use monomeric membrane IgM/IgD with Igα/Igβ, while conventional TCR uses α/β chains with CD3.

questions.text: Which of the following acts as an antigen receptor on naive mature B lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Naive mature B cells coexpress membrane IgM and IgD sharing the same antigen specificity.

questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins is found in serum in low concentrations and is present on the surface of naive B lymphocytes as an antigen receptor?
questions.explanation: IgD is low in serum and coexpressed with IgM on naive B cells, but it does have demonstrated biological functions.

questions.text: Which of the following cells have the ability to produce antibodies
questions.explanation: Activated B cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells; T and NK cells do not produce antibodies.

questions.text: Igα and Igβ that present in mature B cell. Responsible for
options: It acts as signal transducing molecules
It attaches to the antigen of microorganism
questions.explanation: Igα/Igβ transduce BCR signals rather than binding antigen or becoming secreted antitoxin.

questions.text: Compare between the BCR and TCR
questions.modelAnswer: BCR is membrane immunoglobulin with paired heavy/light chains and Igα/Igβ signaling subunits; it binds native soluble or surface antigens including nonproteins. Conventional TCR is αβ with CD3/ζ signaling and recognizes peptide-MHC with CD4 or CD8 coreceptors. Both undergo receptor gene rearrangement and clonal selection; antibody can be secreted and undergo class switching/affinity maturation, while TCR is not secreted or class-switched.
questions.explanation: BCR is membrane immunoglobulin with paired heavy/light chains and Igα/Igβ signaling subunits; it binds native soluble or surface antigens including nonproteins. Conventional TCR is αβ with CD3/ζ signaling and recognizes peptide-MHC with CD4 or CD8 coreceptors. Both undergo receptor gene rearrangement and clonal selection; antibody can be secreted and undergo class switching/affinity maturation, while TCR is not secreted or class-switched.

questions.text: Molecules associated with B cells Ag receptors are called?
questions.explanation: Igα/Igβ provide BCR signal-transducing ITAMs; the other names do not identify the signaling heterodimer.

questions.text: Concerning maturation of B lymphocytes:
options: Does not ensure self MHC restriction
Produces cells with IgD and IgM as B cells receptors
questions.explanation: B cells mature in marrow, acquire IgM/IgD and undergo self-reactivity selection without T-cell-style self-MHC restriction.

questions.text: BCR in comparison with TCR?
options: No need for signal transducer molecule
questions.explanation: BCR binds native carbohydrate antigen; conventional TCR requires peptide-MHC and both receptors need signaling subunits.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules can serve as signal transduction molecules on B cells
questions.explanation: Igα and Igβ transduce BCR signals; surface IgM/IgD bind antigen and Fc is not the BCR signaling pair.

questions.text: Which of the following substances enhances the switch from immunoglobulin G(IgG) to immunoglobulin E (IgE) production?
questions.explanation: IL-4 provides a helper cytokine signal favouring B-cell switching to IgE.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules is more efficient in producing a secondary immune response (isotype switching or affinity maturation)?
questions.explanation: Protein antigens such as diphtheria toxin recruit peptide-specific T-cell help and support affinity maturation and class-switched recall.

questions.text: Repeated exposure to a protein antigen leads to production of antibodies with a better capability of binding with antigens. This process is called;
questions.explanation: Affinity maturation increases average antibody binding strength through variable-region mutation and selection of higher-affinity B cells.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is involved in class switching of IgM to IgE:
questions.explanation: IL-4 promotes switching toward IgE in B cells receiving appropriate helper activation.

questions.text: Which of the following cytokines is involved in class switching of IgM to IgA:
questions.explanation: TGF-β promotes IgA class switching; IL-5 supports secretion/differentiation after switching. This is the best listed pair, while both signals should not be described as identical switch factors.

questions.text: Isotype class switching of immunoglobulins is mediated by
options: Recognition of PAMPs on microbes by Toll-like receptors on B cells
CD40L / CD-40 interactions on T helper and B cells respectively
Recognition of deposited C3b on pathogen by B cells
questions.explanation: CD40L on helper T cells binds B-cell CD40 with cytokines to direct class switching; BCR recognition/processing and innate ligands alone are different signals.

questions.text: Isotype classes resulting from a single clone of B lymphocytes differ in :
options: Variable region of both heavy and light chain
questions.explanation: Isotype switching replaces the heavy-chain constant region while retaining the same antigen-binding variable regions and light chain.

questions.text: CD40L/CD40 interaction between T helper and B cells is important for:
questions.explanation: CD40-CD40L directly supports class switching; uncoupled capsular polysaccharides can elicit antibodies without this T-cell help, and the interaction is activating rather than inhibitory.

questions.text: The phenomenon of affinity maturation of antibodies occurring in prolonged and repeated infections is due to:
options: High mutation rate of proliferating B cells at late phase of humoral immune response
PAMPs on microbes acting on Toll like receptors on B-lymphocytes
Complement component (C3d) acting on complement receptor 2 on B lymphocytes
Costimulation of B lymphocytes by CD28 on macrophages
questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation followed by selection increases antibody affinity; TLR/co-receptor signals are activation inputs and CD28 is not macrophage B-cell costimulation.

questions.text: Affinity maturation of antibodies at the late phase of humoral immune response is due to mutations in:
questions.explanation: Affinity-altering somatic mutations affect variable regions, rather than heavy/light constant-domain genes.

questions.text: In a patient who later developed an allergy to a certain antigen, the initial response to the antigen consisted of immunoglobulin of the IgM class, However, overtime, antigen specific IgE came to be predominant. This change from an IgM to an IgE response is caused by
questions.explanation: IgM-to-IgE changes heavy-chain constant class by isotype switching; affinity mutations or allelic exclusion do not themselves change the isotype.

questions.text: Accumulation of point mutations that affect light and heavy chain variable regions causing an increase in antibody binding to its specific antigen is termed
questions.explanation: Affinity maturation selects antibodies binding the original antigen more strongly after somatic mutation; tolerance/anergy suppress and mimicry cross-reacts.

questions.text: In isotype switching of an antibody
options: The idiotype of the antibody is changed
The constant region of heavy chain is changed
The binding affinity of the antibody is increased
Accelerated mutation of DNA coding within hypervariable region
The constant region of antibody molecule is not affected
questions.explanation: Class switching alters the heavy constant region while preserving idiotype; increased affinity comes from variable mutation/selection, not switching itself.

questions.text: Which of the following isn't a result of class switch?
options: Production of AB with different function and properties
questions.explanation: Class switching changes the heavy-chain constant region and effector function while preserving antigen-binding specificity.

questions.text: Isotype switch of produced Abs requires engagement of which of the following molecules?
questions.explanation: CD40-CD40L with cytokines drives isotype switching; B7-CD28 primarily costimulates T cells.

questions.text: CD40 & CD40L interaction is important for
questions.explanation: CD40-CD40L supports APC licensing, B-cell memory development and class switching, so the combined option is best.

questions.text: Which class of antibody crosses the placenta in pregnant women?
questions.explanation: Maternal IgG is actively transported across the placenta and supplies temporary passive protection to the newborn.

questions.text: Which class of antibody is predominant in external secretions as breast milk, tears and saliva?
questions.explanation: Secretory dimeric IgA dominates external mucosal secretions and blocks microbial adherence and toxins.

questions.text: Isotypes are
options: Different antibody classes based on differences in light chain structure
Different antibody classes based on differences in heavy chain structure
Different antibody classes based on differences in both heavy and light chain structure
Different antibody classes based on difference in the Idiotype of the antibody
Different antibody classes based on differences in the hinge region
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin class is determined by the constant region of the heavy chain.

questions.text: In a person infected with RSV, which class of antibody could protect the respiratory mucosa from viral infection?
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA is the principal mucosal antibody protecting respiratory epithelial surfaces.

questions.text: The class of an immunoglobulin is determined by:
options: Class I and Class II major histocompatibility complex proteins
The carbohydrate attached to the light chain is
questions.explanation: The constant heavy-chain type determines the antibody class.

questions.text: Which immunoglobulin has a highest level in a normal 1- day old infant?
questions.explanation: Maternal IgG transported across the placenta makes IgG the predominant serum antibody in a normal newborn.

questions.text: The appropriate immune response in a person with helminthic infection with Trichinella spiralis worm constitutes formation of .
questions.explanation: Helminth defence classically recruits IgE-associated type 2 responses, including mast cells and eosinophils.

questions.text: The relative level of specific Ig M antibodies is of diagnostic significance because:
options: IgM is easier to detect than the other isotypes
Viral infections often results in very high Immunoglobulin response
IgM antibodies are more often protective against reinfection than are the other isotypes
High levels of IgM often correlate with a first recent exposure to the inducing agent
It is the only immunoglobulin that crosses the placenta
questions.explanation: Pathogen-specific IgM commonly accompanies an initial/recent immune response, although persistence and assay limitations prevent a universal timing rule.

questions.text: Regarding IgG, which one of the following is the MOST accurate?
options: Each IgG molecule has one antigen binding site
It is the most antigen receptor in the surface of naive B lymphocytes
During the primary response, it is made in larger amounts than IgM
The ability of IgG to fix complement resides on the constant region of the light chain
Itis the only immunoglobulin that is transferred from mother to fetus in utero
questions.explanation: IgG is actively transported across the placenta, unlike the other principal antibody classes.

questions.text: Which one of the following is a function of humoral mediated immunity?
options: Activate the alternative pathway of complement activation
Inhibit the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Inhibit growth of virally infected cells by enhancing the production of perforins
Activate the Manan lectin pathway of complement activation
questions.explanation: Antibodies neutralize extracellular microbial toxins; control of intracellular mycobacteria and infected host cells predominantly uses cellular immunity.

questions.text: IgG is the only immunoglobulin capable of :
questions.explanation: IgG is the principal antibody class transported across the placenta; other listed functions are shared with other antibody classes.

questions.text: In a patient with Neisseria meningitidis septicemia, which is the MOST appropriate immune response expected to save the patient from this condition?
questions.explanation: Anti-capsular antibodies promote opsonization and complement-dependent clearance of extracellular encapsulated meningococci.

questions.text: IgA is the first line of defense against infections at the mucous membranes. Which of the following statements most accurately describes IgA?
options: Complement fixation tests for IgA will be positive if specific IgA is present
IgA can be destroyed by bacterial proteases produced by certain bacterial species
IgA is not found in saliva, therefore an IgA diagnostic test on saliva will be of no value
IgA is a small molecule with monomeric form only
questions.explanation: Certain bacteria produce IgA proteases; IgA is present in colostrum/saliva and has polymeric secretory forms, not only monomers.

questions.text: All of the following is true about Ig except
options: IgM has 5 Fc portion and 10 Fab portion
IgD present only as surface receptor
IgE mediates the immunity to parasite by attachment to eosinophil by ADCC
IgG mediates immunity to parasite with eosinophil
questions.explanation: IgD can be secreted as well as surface-expressed, so only surface receptor is too absolute; IgM pentamer structure and eosinophil antibody effects are real.

questions.text: All of the following are true about IgG except
options: It mediates the secondary immune response
It is present as receptor on the surface of the memory B cell
The minor antibody in the body
questions.explanation: IgG dominates serum, contributes to secondary responses and opsonization, and can be memory-B-cell surface Ig; minor antibody is false.

questions.text: Which of the following antibody isotype and biological functions are correctly paired?
options: IgE: defense against parasite & binds to mast cells
IgA: 1st antibody to be secreted by B lymphocytes
IgG: present in minute amounts in serum
questions.explanation: IgE binds mast cells and aids helminth defense; IgA crosses mucosa, IgM is secreted first, and IgG dominates serum.

questions.text: Most abundant antibody in colostrum is:
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA is the predominant colostral antibody, rather than IgM, IgG or IgE.

questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins can serve as a marker for intrauterine infections
questions.explanation: Fetal IgM can indicate congenital infection because maternal IgM does not cross placenta; maternal IgG does.

questions.text: Which of the following immunoglobulins can protect respiratory mucosa from viral infections
questions.explanation: Secretory IgA protects respiratory mucosa; IgG dominates serum rather than mucosal secretion.

questions.text: On a primary exposure to an extracellular pathogenic bacteria, humoral immunity is stimulated and the first class of Immunoglobulin to be synthesized is
questions.explanation: IgM is the first major secreted antibody class in a primary humoral response.

questions.text: A 19 year old college student develops a rash. His blood is tested for specific antibodies to chickenpox. Which of the following antibody classes would you expect to find if he is immune to chicken pox?
questions.explanation: Specific IgG commonly marks prior varicella exposure or vaccination and is the usual serologic class assessed for immunity.

questions.text: The capacity to develop a secondary humoral immune response depends on
questions.explanation: Classical T-dependent recall humoral immunity uses both memory B cells and memory helper T cells.

questions.text: In comparison with primary humoral immune response, secondary humoral immune response is characterized by:
options: IgG is the main isotype produced.
IgM is the main isotype produced.
The need for greater dose of stimulating antigen.
Thymus dependent and independent antigens are included.
questions.explanation: Secondary humoral responses typically produce more high-affinity class-switched antibody, often IgG, with a shorter lag than primary responses.

questions.text: Regarding the primary and secondary immune responses, which one of the following is MOST accurate?
options: The IgM made in the primary response is made primarily by memory B cells
The lag phase in the primary response is shorter than in the secondary response
In the primary response, memory B cells are produced but memory T cells are not
The amount of IgG made in secondary response is greater than that in primary response
The amount of IgG made in primary response and secondary response is constant, so no difference is detected between both responses as regards IgG amounts
questions.explanation: Memory-driven secondary responses produce more IgG with less delay than a first response.

questions.text: On second exposure to a hapten/protein conjugate which of the following immune events is expected to occur?
options: Formation of antibodies that are less efficient in preventing specific disease
Decreased antibody binding to the original hapten/protein complex
Maintenance of the same class of antibody produced during primary response
questions.explanation: Repeated exposure to a T-dependent hapten-carrier can select higher-affinity antibody; recall generally increases speed/titer and can include switching rather than fixed class.

questions.text: Which antibody is the predominant antibody in the secondary immune response, and has the greatest concentration of the five immunoglobulins in the fetus?
questions.explanation: IgG commonly dominates switched secondary responses and is selectively transported across placenta; IgM/IgA/IgD/IgE do not cross normally.

A secondary response recruits memory cells, giving a shorter lag, greater and more sustained antibody production, and often higher-affinity class-switched antibody such as IgG. The dominant isotype depends on antigen and tissue.

questions.text: In comparison with primary humoral immune response, 2ry humoral immune response is characterized by:
options: Needs larger amount of Ag to be stimulated
Can be induced by both thymus dependent and thymus independent Ags
questions.explanation: Secondary responses develop faster; they need less antigen and feature high-affinity switched antibodies rather than extra IgM.

Alternative activation begins through C3 tickover and amplification on permissive microbial surfaces; it does not require specific antibody. All converge on C3 activation.

questions.text: The lectin pathway of complement activation is triggered by:
options: Binding of MBL with microbial carbohydrates as mannose
Binding of CRP with microbial carbohydrates
Factor H binding to microbial surfaces
questions.explanation: MBL binds microbial mannose and recruits MASP; CRP/antibody can initiate classical and C3b/factors mediate alternative regulation.

questions.text: All of the following complements are required in the alternative pathway except:
questions.explanation: The alternative activation cascade bypasses C1/C2/C4 and uses C3/factors with properdin; its downstream terminal pathway includes C5-C9.

questions.text: Regarding the complement pathway, which one of the following is the MOST accurate?
options: C3 convertase protects normal cells from lysis by complement
C3a is a decay acceleration factor and causes the rapid decay of bacteria
Gram positive bacteria are more likely to be killed by complement than Gram negative
The membrane attack complex is formed as a result of activation of the classic pathway, but not by activation of the alternative pathway
The first time a person is exposed to a microorganism, the alternative pathway is more likely to be activated than the classic pathway.
questions.explanation: Without induced specific antibody, innate alternative activation is a reasonable first-exposure route; MAC can follow every pathway and Gram-negative membranes are more susceptible.

questions.text: All of the following activates the alternative pathway except
questions.explanation: LPS, microbial surfaces and fungi favor alternative activation; immune complexes classically initiate C1-dependent activation before alternative amplification.

questions.text: The alternative pathway of complement is characterized by the functions listed below except:
options: Activation of complement components beyond C3 in the cascade
Generation of chemotactic factors for neutrophils
questions.explanation: Alternative activation bypasses C4 while generating downstream C3/C5 products, inflammatory peptides and terminal MAC with properdin stabilization.

questions.text: The classical pathway of complement begins with
options: Cleavage and activation of C4, C2 and C3
IgA binding to a specific epitope
questions.explanation: Classical activation starts with C1, then C4/C2 and C3; IgA is not its usual trigger and MAC is downstream.

questions.text: Complement is a series of important host proteins that provides protection against invasion by foreign microorganisms. Which of the following statements best describe complement?
options: Complement is activated by IgE antibody classes
Complement plays a minor role in the inflammatory response
Microorganisms agglutinate in the presence of complement but do not lyse
Complement protects the host from pneumococcal infection through C1,C2 and C4
questions.explanation: Early classical complement contributes to protection against encapsulated pneumococci; complement enhances uptake/inflammation and can lyse targets rather than IgE activation or inhibition.

questions.text: Which of the following complement pathways is related to humoral immunity:
questions.explanation: The classical pathway couples antigen-antibody complexes to complement; lectin and alternative activation do not require specific antibody.

questions.text: Enumerate 3 immunological functions of complement
questions.modelAnswer: C3b and iC3b coat microbes and promote phagocytosis through complement receptors. C3a and C5a promote inflammation, and C5a recruits/activates leukocytes. C5b–C9 forms the membrane attack complex, which can lyse susceptible microbes.
points: C3b and iC3b coat microbes and promote phagocytosis through complement receptors.
C3a and C5a promote inflammation, and C5a recruits/activates leukocytes.
C5b–C9 forms the membrane attack complex, which can lyse susceptible microbes.
questions.explanation: C3b and iC3b coat microbes and promote phagocytosis through complement receptors. C3a and C5a promote inflammation, and C5a recruits/activates leukocytes. C5b–C9 forms the membrane attack complex, which can lyse susceptible microbes.

questions.text: Which of the following outcomes is expected to occur after complement activation
questions.explanation: Complement deposits C3b to enhance phagocytosis; it is not primarily toxin neutralization, antibody-dependent killing or T-cell proliferation.

questions.text: Removal of harmful immune complexes from the body is done by :
questions.explanation: C3b-tagged complexes bind complement receptors for clearance; C3a/C5a are inflammatory fragments and C1q initiates recognition.

questions.text: Of the following which one is the most important function of the complex formed by (C5b,6,7,8,9)?
options: To release histamine from mast cells
questions.explanation: C5b-C9 forms membrane attack pores; C3b opsonizes and C3a/C5a induce inflammatory mediator release.

questions.text: Which of the following complement components is closely related in function to an anaphylatoxin?
questions.explanation: C3a is an anaphylatoxin; C3b opsonizes, C1 initiates classical cleavage and C2 is a convertase enzyme component.

questions.text: Which of the following complement component is the most chemotactic for neutrophils?
questions.explanation: C5a is the most potent listed neutrophil chemoattractant; C3a/C4a are weaker and C3b/C5b have other principal functions.

questions.text: Which of the following complement components is an opsonin:
questions.explanation: C3b is a major opsonin; C3a/C5a are inflammatory peptides and C5b initiates MAC.

questions.text: C3a is considered an
options: Decay accelerating factor causing the rapid decay of bacteria
questions.explanation: C3a is an anaphylatoxin, not an opsonin, DAF or regulatory/acute-phase protein.

questions.text: Of the following, which one is the most important function of complement components C5b, 6, 7, 8, 9?
options: To release histamine from mast cells
questions.explanation: The C5b-C9 MAC damages microbial membranes; opsonization and histamine-release functions belong mainly to other complement fragments.

questions.text: A 56 year old alcoholic man who is a heavy smoker is brought to the emergency room due to dyspnea and difficulty in breathing. He is febrile and endotracheal aspirates show a mucopurulent discharge containing numerous Gram positive cocci in chains. His serum contains high titers of IgM antibodies specific for the polysaccharide capsule of Streptococcus pneumoniae. The effector mechanism most likely to act in concert with the early IgM production to clear infection is
questions.explanation: IgM fixes complement; deposited C3 fragments promote bacterial phagocytosis.

questions.text: Which of the following complement components plays a role in immune complex clearance
questions.explanation: C3b tags immune complexes for clearance; C5a recruits cells, C5b initiates MAC and MASP begins lectin cleavage.

questions.text: Mention mechanisms of complement activity regulation giving an example of each
questions.modelAnswer: Initiation is limited by C1 inhibitor, which inactivates C1r/C1s. Convertases are destabilized by decay-accelerating factor (CD55) or factor H. Factor I cleaves C3b/C4b with cofactors such as MCP/CD46, CR1 or factor H. Terminal attack is restricted by CD59, which prevents MAC assembly on host cells.

Convertases are destabilized by decay-accelerating factor (CD55) or factor H.
Factor I cleaves C3b/C4b with cofactors such as MCP/CD46, CR1 or factor H.
Terminal attack is restricted by CD59, which prevents MAC assembly on host cells.

questions.text: Repeated Neisseria meningitidis septicemia in an individual should raise clinician awareness to what?
questions.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria strongly suggests a terminal complement/MAC defect, unlike broad T-cell failure, neutropenia or C1-inhibitor angioedema.

questions.text: Individuals with a genetic deficiency of C6 have:
questions.explanation: C6 loss prevents MAC assembly and raises Neisseria susceptibility; it does not chiefly cause viral resistance loss, hypersensitivity, cancer or autoimmunity.

questions.text: Patients with severely reduced C3 levels tend to have:
options: Increased numbers of severe viral infections
Increased numbers of severe pyogenic infections
Loss of delayed hypersensitivity reaction to Tuberculin
questions.explanation: Severe C3 depletion disrupts opsonization and predisposes to pyogenic bacterial infections, rather than selectively impairing T-cell DTH.

questions.text: Which of the following is a complement control protein?
questions.explanation: CD59 protects against terminal MAC; CD28/CD4/CD8 are T-cell signaling/coreceptor molecules and CD95 is Fas.

questions.text: Which of the following cell surface molecules is essential for protecting normal cells from lysis by complement
questions.explanation: DAF is a cell-membrane convertase-decay regulator; CRP/MBL/C1 inhibitor are soluble and factor B promotes alternative activation.

questions.text: Which of the following complement regulatory proteins works by inhibiting polymerization of C9 in membrane attack complex
questions.explanation: CD59 blocks C9 incorporation/polymerization; DAF/H decay convertases while properdin and factor B promote activation.

questions.text: A 31 year old man is treated for a fourth episode of disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection in the last 5 years. He had no history of unusual or recurrent infections. If he has an immunological defect, which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Selective recurrent disseminated Neisseria in an otherwise well adult suggests terminal C8 deficiency; SCID/DiGeorge and antibody deficiencies have wider phenotypes.

questions.text: Patients with C5 through C9 complement deficiencies are most likely to be susceptible to which of the following infections?
questions.explanation: Terminal C5-C9 defects preferentially predispose to Neisseria because MAC killing is impaired; IgA/B-cell or T-cell defects fit other pathogens.

questions.text: A serum protein that helps in regulating complement activity is:
questions.explanation: Factor I is a plasma regulatory protease; DAF is membrane-bound, properdin stabilizes convertase, and sialic acid is not a protein.

questions.text: DAF protects self cells from complement activation by:
questions.explanation: DAF accelerates convertase decay by dissociating the enzyme component; factor I cleaves C3b and CD59 restrains MAC.

questions.text: Compare breifly between Active and passive immuniozation "in 2 points"
questions.modelAnswer: Active immunization supplies antigen to stimulate the recipient's own response; protection develops over time and usually generates immunological memory. Passive immunization supplies preformed antibody; protection is immediate but temporary, and transferred antibody does not create the recipient's own antigen-specific memory.

questions.text: The best way to provide immunological protection against tetanus neonaturom of a newborn is to:
options: Inject the newborn with human tetanus antitoxin
Inject the newborn with tetanus toxoid
Inject the mother with toxoid within 72 hours of the birth of her child
Immunize the mother with tetanus toxoid before or early in pregnancy
Give the newborn antitoxin and toxoid for both passive and active immunization
questions.explanation: Maternal immunity before delivery provides transplacental antitoxin to protect the newborn.

questions.text: The main advantage of passive immunization is that
questions.explanation: Transferred antibody protects immediately.

questions.text: The protection against Mycobacterium tuberculosis afforded by BCG vaccination is an example of
questions.explanation: Vaccination induces the recipient’s own adaptive response.

questions.text: A man was struck by a car and his leg was crushed. The condition necessitates amputation above knee. Although the man had taken a booster dose of tetanus toxoid 6 years ago, he was revaccinated and antitetanus immunoglobulin was injected around the macerated tissue. Administration of immunoglobulin is an example of which of the following forms of immunization?
questions.explanation: Administered preformed antitoxin is artificial passive immunization; it does not stimulate the recipient to generate an adaptive response to tetanus. The separate toxoid is not the intervention asked about.

questions.text: A mother and her newborn are exposed to a pathogen while at the hospital for routine checkup. The same pathogen had infected the mother a year previously, and she had recovered successfully from the subsequent illness. Which of the following describes acquired immunity with respect to the new born?
questions.explanation: Maternal antibody provides natural passive protection to a newborn.

questions.text: A 5 year old child arrives at the emergency department minutes after bitten by a black widow spider. Anti-venom immunoglobulins are injected immediately to the child. What type of immunization does this injection present?
questions.explanation: Injected antivenom is a prepared antibody product.

questions.text: What is the type of protection resulting from recovery from infection?
questions.explanation: Recovery stimulates the person's own adaptive response and memory, so it is naturally acquired active immunity.

questions.text: What is the main advantage of passive immunization over active immunization?
options: Antibody persists for a longer period
There is no fear of allergic reaction
questions.explanation: Transferred antibodies act immediately but are temporary, can cause reactions and do not chiefly contain IgM or rely on oral delivery.

questions.text: Enumerate 3 types of vacines
questions.modelAnswer: Examples of vaccine types are live attenuated vaccines, inactivated whole-organism vaccines, and subunit vaccines containing selected proteins or polysaccharides. subQuestions.explanation: Recombinant subunit vaccine: antigen is produced in an expression host.

subQuestions.text: Genes coding for Ag insertd into non cytopathic virus:

subQuestions.explanation: Viral-vector vaccine: a safe vector delivers an antigen-encoding gene.

subQuestions.text: Genitically engineered mRNA Coding specefic viral protein:

subQuestions.text: Plasmid DNA encoding Antigenic proteins injected into recepient:

subQuestions.explanation: DNA vaccine: a plasmid encodes antigen for production in host cells.

questions.text: What is a toxoid?
options: An inactivated form of a toxin having one or more epitopes in common with it
A substance that augments the immune response against the toxin
A toxin that is conjugated to a carrier protein
A substance that enhances the immunogenicity of the toxin
A toxin that is conjugated to an inert latex particle
questions.explanation: A toxoid is detoxified toxin retaining antigenicity.

questions.text: In active immunization, converting a toxin to a toxoid is done to
options: Decrease the toxigenicity of the toxin while retaining the immunogenic epitopes
Decease the toxigenicity of the toxin and enhance its immunogenicity
Convert it to a hapten / carrier conjugate
questions.explanation: Detoxification preserves antigenic epitopes for protective immunization.

questions.text: Adjuvants administered with vaccines indirectly augment the immune response by;
options: Stimulating NADPH oxidase enzyme so, increase reactive O2 species production in APCs
Upregulation of interleukin receptors on T lymphocytes
Improve antibody affinity to the antigen
Attraction of APCs and increase their expression of costimulatory molecules
Binding to intracellular receptors resulting in enhanced gene transcription
questions.explanation: Adjuvants improve antigen presentation and innate activation at immunization.

questions.text: Which one of the followings describes a common use of adjuvant?
options: Enhancement of the effect of vaccines
questions.explanation: An adjuvant strengthens vaccine immunogenicity.

questions.text: An immunological adjuvant is a substance that:
options: Reduces the toxicity of the immunogen
Enhances the immune response against an immunogen
questions.explanation: Adjuvants amplify the immune response to a coadministered immunogen.

questions.text: A very important goal of vaccination is production of?
questions.explanation: Long-term vaccine protection depends on immunological memory.

questions.text: Which of the following vaccines could be taken in an immunocompromised host?
questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines can be used in immunocompromised patients; live vaccines may be contraindicated.

questions.text: Which of the following vaccines is a hapten carrier conjugate
questions.explanation: Hib conjugate vaccine attaches polysaccharide antigen to protein.

questions.text: Vaccination for varicella (chicken pox) is reported to be 95% effective in preventing serious disease. Some studies indicate that immunity lasts at least 20 years after vaccination. Based on these findings, the type of vaccine used for varicella is most likely
questions.explanation: The named varicella vaccine is live attenuated; the question is answerable from the vaccine identity, while duration alone is not a general classifier.

questions.text: Which of the following describes a common use of adjuvant
options: Stimulate apoptosis so used in suppression of tumor growth
questions.explanation: Adjuvants improve vaccine immunogenicity.

questions.text: Which of the following substances if introduced with a vaccine, would serve the purpose of attracting neutrophilic infiltrate to the area?
questions.explanation: IL-8 is a direct neutrophil chemoattractant.

questions.text: IL-8 is added to a vaccine to attract neutrophils to the injection site. In this context, the added substance serves as which of the following?
questions.explanation: A coadministered substance that augments vaccine responses acts as an adjuvant.

questions.text: A 14 month old boy who has not received any recommended vaccines remains healthy despite his daily association with several other children for the past year at a home day care facility. Which of the following mechanisms BEST explains why he has not contracted diphtheria, measles, pertussis or polio?
questions.explanation: High community immunity can indirectly protect an unvaccinated child.

questions.text: Which of the following types of vaccines would most likely evoke the best and most long-lasting protective immune response against measles?
questions.explanation: The effective measles vaccines are live attenuated and induce durable immunity.

questions.text: The process of weakening a pathogen is called
questions.explanation: Attenuation means weakening virulence; vaccination and immunization are administration/protection terms.

questions.text: A vaccine can be
questions.explanation: Vaccines can contain antigenic protein or attenuated/otherwise weakened organisms; these are distinct platforms.

questions.text: Which of the following statement is true regarding vaccination
options: Vaccination is a method of active immunisation
Vaccination is a method of passive immunisation
Vaccination is a method of artificial passive immunisation
Vaccination is a method of natural passive immunisation
questions.explanation: Vaccination stimulates active immunity; it does not provide natural or artificial passive antibody transfer.

questions.text: Example for recombinant antigen vaccine approved for human use is
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B surface antigen is produced recombinantly; the other listed conventional vaccines use other platforms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example for live attenuated vaccine
questions.explanation: Sabin oral polio is live attenuated; Salk is inactivated, hepatitis B antigen recombinant and Pfizer mRNA nonlive.

questions.text: Which of the following is a polysaccharide vaccine
questions.explanation: Hib vaccine contains capsular polysaccharide conjugated to carrier protein; anthrax is antigen/toxoid based and rabies/hepatitis A are viral.

questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms does Pfizer Covid 19 vaccine act by:
options: Injection of viral DNA inside nanoparticles which is integrated to host genome
Injection of sensitized lymphocytes against Covid 19
Injection of mRNA inside nanoparticles which is expressed by host cells
questions.explanation: Lipid-delivered mRNA is translated by host cells; it is not killed virus, integrated DNA or transferred sensitized lymphocytes.

questions.text: A depressed level of MHC class I molecules on host cells is recognized in
questions.explanation: Adenovirus E3/19K retains MHC-I intracellularly and reduces cell-surface presentation; CGD affects oxidative killing and the other diseases do not define this evasion mechanism.

questions.text: The earliest event in an effective immune response against a viral infection is:
questions.explanation: Type I interferon is an early innate antiviral response; antibody and adaptive cytotoxic responses take longer and classical antibody activation is later.

questions.text: Which of the following molecules is produced early in the course of viral infection and serves to slow the infection of adjoining cells
questions.explanation: Type I interferon induces an antiviral state in neighboring cells.

questions.text: A 7 year old child presents to the clinic with severe headache, sinus congestion, fever, sore throat and cough. Respiratory secretions reveal high levels of the cytokine interferon. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this cytokine?
options: Binds extracellular viral particles and prevents cellular adherence
Upregulates the synthesis of secretory proteins that bind and inhibit the virus particles
Disrupts viral and cellular protein synthesis, leading to cellular apoptosis
Inhibits viral protein synthesis by degrading viral mRNA
Decreases levels of viral receptors on the cytoplasmic membrane
questions.explanation: Interferon induces host enzymes that degrade viral RNA and inhibit translation.

questions.text: A small child presents with low grade fever, flu, sore throat and a bright red rash on his body. Elevated IgG and IgM antibody titers to parvovirus suggest a diagnosis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease.

questions.text: A 70-year-old man develops encephalitis due to infection with West Nile virus and astrocytes become infected by the virus. These astrocytes no longer express MHC class I antigen. Which of the following inflammatory cells is most likely to destroy these infected astrocytes?
questions.explanation: Missing MHC I renders virally infected targets susceptible to NK killing.

questions.text: A 52-year-old woman has had malaise with fever and non-productive cough for 4 weeks, Her temperature is 37.8°C. A chest radiograph shows upper lobe cavitation along with infiltrates and focal calcifications. Which is the cytokine produced by the cell regulating this response?
questions.explanation: A tuberculous granulomatous response is regulated by Th1-derived IFN-gamma activating macrophages.

questions.text: Viruses can evade immune system by which of the following mechanisms
questions.explanation: Viruses use antigenic mutation, MHC-I downregulation and immunomodulatory IL-10 homologues to escape host defense.

questions.text: Type I interferons play an important role in innate immunity against:
questions.explanation: Type I interferons induce antiviral states, rather than specializing in intracellular bacterial or fungal killing.

questions.text: Parasites can evade immune response by:
options: Induce T regulatory production of IL-10
questions.explanation: Parasites evade through protective surface structures, antigenic variation and immune suppression.

questions.text: Which of the following cell doesn't mediate immunity to virus
questions.explanation: Eosinophils primarily mediate helminth/type-2 defense; macrophages, Th1 and cytotoxic cells participate in antiviral defense.

questions.text: Extracellular bacteria can be effectively cleared through which of the following?
options: Apoptosis induced by cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Th17 cells promote defence against extracellular bacteria and fungi through IL-17-associated recruitment of phagocytes.

questions.text: Regarding antibody-mediated immunity and cell mediated immunity, which one of the following is the most accurate?
options: Antibody-mediated immunity helps to prevent graft rejection
Antibody-mediated immunity protects against anaphylactic shock
Antibody-mediated immunity protects against autoimmune diseases
Cell mediated immunity neutralizes extracellular viruses
Cell mediated immunity protects against fungal infections
questions.explanation: Cell-mediated responses defend against fungal infection; antibodies instead neutralize extracellular virions and can mediate graft rejection, allergy and autoimmunity.

questions.text: Cells responsible of granuloma formation in chronic Brucellosis are
questions.explanation: Th1 IFN-γ activates macrophages that organize granulomatous defense against persistent intracellular Brucella; Th2/eosinophil or basophil pairs are not the granuloma program.

questions.text: In an intracellular bacterial infection, which of the following adaptive immune responses is most important?
questions.explanation: Among the listed responses, cytotoxic T cells are the only adaptive cellular mechanism.

questions.text: In a leukemic patient on cytotoxic drugs fungal infections as candidemia is expected. A defect in which of the following cells is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-associated neutropenia strongly predisposes to invasive candidemia.

questions.text: The earliest immune events to combat an extracellular bacterial infection are:
options: Phagocytosis and altemative complement pathway activation
questions.explanation: Early phagocyte and complement activity precedes antigen-specific antibody production.

questions.text: Which of the following is the MOST important in defense against the pulmonary tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Th1-mediated macrophage activation provides the central defense against pulmonary tuberculosis.

questions.text: The main protective immunity against mycobacterium tuberculosis is done by:
questions.explanation: Activated antigen-specific T cells control mycobacterial infection.

questions.text: In a patient with Salmonella infection, which of the following mechanisms will most likely be the earliest adaptive response for clearing the infection while bacteria are present within intracellular endosomes?
options: Antibody mediated neutralization of free bacteria
Complement mediated lysis of infected host cells
Cytotoxic T lymphocyte recognition of bacteria peptides presented by MHC I
Delayed type hypersensitivity responses generated by CD4 T cells
Type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE antibodies
questions.explanation: Intravesicular Salmonella requires CD4-mediated macrophage activation.

questions.text: Which of the following pathogens elicit a TH-1 response?
questions.explanation: Mycobacteria in macrophage vesicles favor protective Th1 responses.

questions.text: All of the following elicit a TH-1 response EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: H influenzae is a primarily extracellular encapsulated pathogen, unlike the listed intracellular agents.

questions.text: Mycobacterium TB bacteria can resist IC killing by macrophages as it:
questions.explanation: Tubercle bacilli inhibit phagosome maturation/fusion; simple phagosomal escape is not the standard mechanism.

questions.text: Recurrent mucocutaneous candidal infections is associated with deficiency in?
questions.explanation: Th17/IL-17 defects predispose to mucocutaneous Candida; Th1, Th2 or CD8 deficiency alone does not match the tested association.

questions.text: Capsule is a structure made by some bacteria to evade immune system, as it's?
options: Inhibits bone marrow production of leukocytes
questions.explanation: Capsules impede phagocytosis and can protect against complement and antibody access; the other choices do not describe standard capsule actions.

questions.text: All of the following cells mediate immunity to fungus or extracellular bacteria except
questions.explanation: Th17 and recruited phagocytes protect against extracellular microbes; Th1 is the contrasting canonical intracellular pathway.

questions.text: Which of the following is an effective defense mechanism against extracellular bacteria
options: Antibody mediated opsonization and complement activation
questions.explanation: Antibody opsonization with complement aids phagocytic removal of extracellular bacteria; CTLs and NK specialize in infected host cells.

questions.text: A 45 year old female presents with anorexia and abdominal pain. Fecal smear reveal Taenia solium eggs. Which one of the following cells are most effective in defence against this parasite?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are the characteristic antihelminth effector among these choices; CTL/NK attack host cells and phagocytes cannot engulf adult worms.

questions.text: Which of the following is an immune evasion mechanism by viruses?
questions.explanation: Changing surface antigens lets viruses escape preexisting antibody recognition.

questions.text: A 25 year old man is exposed to the round worm ascaris but does not develop clinical signs of infection. Which of the following mechanisms is likely to be responsible for his resistance to infection?
options: Antibody mediated destruction of worm infected host cells
Cytotoxic T lymphocyte induced apoptosis of worm infected host cells
Complement mediated lysis of worm attached to host tissues
IgE mediated type I hypersensitivity disrupting worm attachment
Phagocytosis of worms followed by necrosis of phagocytes
questions.explanation: IgE-mediated mucosal responses can help expel helminths.

questions.text: Despite having recovered fully from influenza the previous winter, a 56 year old man becomes ill after being exposed to a colleague with influenza virus. Which of the following mechanisms permits his reinfection despite previous exposure to influenza virus?
options: Neutralizing antibodies against influenza disappear rapidly
Insufficient time has passed for CD4 T cells to develop memory
Intracellular viral particles escape immune surveillance
Type I hypersensitivity responses occur on second exposure to influenza
Viral variants evade the immune response against the original virus
questions.explanation: Antigenic variants can escape immunity directed at an earlier influenza strain.

questions.text: A patient with a long history of consuming poorly cooked pig meat presents with generalized myalgia and low grade fever. Striated muscle biopsy reveals multiple cysts. Eosinophilia is prominent. Which of the following immunoglobulin isotypes is MOST likely to be elevated?
questions.explanation: Helminth infection with eosinophilia favors IgE responses.

questions.text: Immunity against protozoa "IC parasites" is mainly mediated by
questions.explanation: Th1 IFN-γ activates macrophages against intracellular protozoa; Th2/eosinophils chiefly target helminths.

questions.text: Immunity against helminths is mediated by?
questions.explanation: Th2-directed IgE and eosinophils mediate helminth defense; Th1/macrophages target intracellular microbes.

questions.text: Which of the following mediate immunity against parasite
questions.explanation: Eosinophils are the standard listed parasite-killing granulocyte; NK/neutrophils primarily target other threats.

questions.text: Which of the following mediate immunity against parasite
questions.explanation: Th2 help, antibodies and eosinophils together contribute to antihelminth immunity, unlike any one alone.

questions.text: Talk about the cells and protein used to defend against virus and parasite
questions.modelAnswer: Viruses: type I IFNs limit replication; NK cells act early, CD8 CTLs kill infected cells, Th1/IFN-γ supports cellular defense and antibodies neutralize extracellular virions. Helminths: Th2 IL-4/IL-13 drive type 2 responses and IgE switching; IL-5 activates/recruits eosinophils; IgE/Fc receptor interactions, eosinophil granules and mast-cell-mediated expulsion aid defense. Protozoa vary by intracellular location and often require Th1 macrophage activation.

Helminths: Th2 IL-4/IL-13 drive type 2 responses and IgE switching; IL-5 activates/recruits eosinophils; IgE/Fc receptor interactions, eosinophil granules and mast-cell-mediated expulsion aid defense. questions.text: give reasons: Immediate type of hypersensitivity requires at least 2 exposures to the allergen

On subsequent exposure, multivalent allergen cross-links this cell-bound IgE and triggers mediator release. Prior sensitization is required, although the earlier exposure may be unrecognized or involve a cross-reacting antigen.

questions.text: In an individual with an immediate hypersensitivity (allergy) to dust mites, crosslinking of which of the following dust-mite-specific molecules will trigger inflammatory mediator release?
questions.explanation: Allergen crosslinks FcεRI-bound specific IgE, releasing mast-cell mediators; histamine is the product, not the crosslinked recognition molecule.

questions.text: While walking through a field, a 28 year old woman is stung be a bee. Within 10 minutes, she has asthmatic-like symptoms. This type of hypersensitivity reaction is characterized by which of the following sequence of steps?
options: Allergen, chemical mediators, sensitization, allergen, IgE, symptoms
Allergen, IgE, sensitization, allergen, chemical mediators, symptoms
Allergen, sensitization, IgE, allergen, chemical mediators, symptoms
Sensitization, allergen, chemical mediators, allergen, IgE, symptoms
Sensitization, IgE, allergen, symptoms, allergen, chemical mediators
questions.explanation: Initial sensitization produces IgE; reexposure activates mediator release.

questions.text: Which of the following hypersensitivity responses are diagnosed by a skin test
questions.explanation: Skin prick and patch tests diagnose immediate and contact hypersensitivity, respectively.

questions.text:
Case context: A 4 year old child suffering from repeated attacks of wheezing and difficulty in breathing, After history taking by his doctor who recognizes that the attacks are induced by contact with a pet in his house, bronchial asthma is suspected, what does he recommend him first to do?

For this case, Which type of hypersensitivity is involved and which are the immune cells involved in its pathogenesis?
options: Delayed type hypersensitivity/ TH1 cells ,Tcytotoxin cells and Macrophages
Type I hypersensitivity/ Th2 cells , Mast cells and Eosinophils
Cytotoxic hypersensitivity/ B lymphocytes and plasma cells
Immune complex hypersensitivity/ B cells and TH2 cells
questions.explanation: Allergic asthma involves type I IgE response with Th2, mast-cell and eosinophil participation.

questions.text: A 36 year old female was stung by a bee. Within minutes she developed respiratory distress and lost consciousness. This represents
questions.explanation: Immediate collapse after a bee sting is IgE-mediated anaphylaxis.
