questions.text: A 12 year old female with a history of IgE mediated allergic response to house dust mites presented with acute bronchial asthma. Which of the following will be most likely to be used FIRST in her treatment?
questions.explanation: An inhaled beta2 agonist rapidly relieves bronchospasm during an acute asthma episode.

questions.text: Atopic persons with a hereditary predisposition to immediate hypersensitivity reactions produce an increased amount of IgE. Of the following, which one is the most likely explanation for the increased production of IgE?
options: Large amounts of IL-1 are produced by dendritic cells
Large amounts of IL-2 are produced by macrophages
Large amounts of IL-4 are produced by Th2 cells
Large amounts of Interferon gamma are produced by Th1 cells
Large amounts of C3a are produced by the alternative pathway of complement
questions.explanation: Th2 cytokines promote IgE class switching.

questions.text: A 45-year-old female had a bee sting on her right hand. She gave a past history of being stung several times. Within 5 minutes, she collapsed and lost consciousness. She was resuscitated and recovered completely by the next day. What is the most appropriate test you recommend for diagnosis?
options: Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) for antigen specific IgE
questions.explanation: Specific IgE testing can identify bee-venom sensitization after anaphylaxis.

questions.text: An allergen is prevented from reacting with a specific IgE molecule on mast cell membrane as a result of therapy with:
questions.explanation: Desensitization promotes allergen-blocking IgG and reduces IgE-mediated reactivity.

questions.text: A patient has episodes of eye tearing ( excessive lacrimation), red eye and runny nose, which you think may be due to an allergy to some plant pollen. You refer the patient to an allergist, who performs skin tests with various allergens. A wheal and flare reaction is seen on the patient’s back at the site where several pollens were injected. What is the most likely sequence of events that produced this reaction?
options: Allergen binds to IgE on the surface of B cells and IL-4 is released
Allergen binds to IgE on the surface of mast cells and histamine is released
Allergen bind to skin proteins and histamine is released
Allergen binds to IgE in the plasma which activates complement to produce C3b
Allergen binds to IgE in plasma, and the allergen IgE complex binds to the surface of macrophages and IL-1 is released
questions.explanation: Skin prick allergen crosslinks mast-cell-bound IgE and releases histamine.

questions.text: A 12 year old female with a history of IgE- mediated responses to various common allergens presents with acute bronchial asthma. Which of the following cells are responsible for immune pathology
options: TH2 cells and T cytotoxic cells
questions.explanation: Th2 polarization and IgE-dependent mast-cell activation underpin allergic asthma.

questions.text: Cells responsible for late phase of allergic reaction of Type I hypersensitivity
options: Mast cells, basophils and TH1 cells
questions.explanation: Late allergic inflammation recruits Th2 cells, eosinophils and basophils.

questions.text: A 25 year old female with a history of penicillin allergy unknown to her physician was given a single injection of penicillin for the treatment of syphilis. Within minutes she developed urticaria, tachycardia, and hypotension. This patient has experienced
questions.explanation: Immediate urticaria and hypotension after penicillin indicates anaphylaxis.

questions.text: A 31 year old woman developed nausea and urticarial rash after eating oysters at a party. No others who attended the party and ate oysters became ill. A month later, she again consumed oysters and developed abdominal pain, vomiting and angioedema (swelling of lips and tongue) in addition to her previous symptoms. In this patient ,oysters functioned as a:
questions.explanation: The oyster proteins elicit antigen-specific allergic immune responses and function as immunogens.

questions.text: A 9 year-old girl is stung on her arm by a bee. The first time she was stung was 2 years ago, the sting site was painful and became swollen but resolved after that. This time however, widespread urticaria (hives) develops soon after the sting. She also develops facial edema and difficulty in breathing. This patient has most likely experienced
questions.explanation: Rapid generalized urticaria and airway compromise after reexposure is anaphylaxis.

questions.text: A 12 year old female with a history of IgE- mediated responses to various common allergens presents with acute bronchial asthma. Which of the following treatment approaches will most likely be used first in her treatment?
questions.explanation: Inhaled beta2 agonists provide rapid relief of acute bronchoconstriction.

questions.text: A previously healthy 45 year old male presents with rhinorrhea, nasal congestion and persistent respiratory symptoms. He has noticed mold growing along the walls of his house. Skin testing for sensitivity to common mold spores gave positive results to several of them in less than 30 minutes. These findings indicate an example of
questions.explanation: Positive skin testing within minutes is immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.text: An 8 year old female with a known allergy to peanuts ingests a cereal containing traces of peanuts. Within 1 hour she develops diffuse erythema of skin and urticarial associated with shortness of breath and wheezing. These findings suggest which of the following events?
options: Fc receptor bearing cells binding to host cells coated with IgG
IgG binding to extracellular matrix of the respiratory passages
IgM- mediated interaction with cell membranes of lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Rapid peanut-associated urticaria and wheeze indicate IgE-mediated type I allergy.

questions.text: Which of the following T lymphocytes play a pathological role in type I hypersensitivity
questions.explanation: Th2 responses support IgE-mediated immediate allergy; Th1/Th17/cytotoxic cells characterize different responses.

questions.text: In desensitization "immunotherapy" of bronchial asthma, blocking Abs type is:
options: IgM that inhibits allergen binding to IgE
IgG that inhibits allergen binding to IgE
IgA that inhibits cross linking of IgE on mast cells
questions.explanation: Allergen-specific IgG can block allergen access to IgE during desensitization; this differs from administered anti-IgE biologics.

questions.text: All of the following are associated with type I hypersensitivity except
options: Release of preformed mediators from mast cells
Formation of active complexes from complement and antibody
A systemic response can cause shock
questions.explanation: Type I allergy releases mast-cell mediators and involves Th2; complement-antibody complexes characterize other hypersensitivities.

questions.text: A type I hypersensitivity involves an initial phase where the patient is exposed to the antigen for the first time. This phase is called:
questions.explanation: Initial exposure creates sensitization; later antigen crosslinking causes degranulation or anaphylaxis, and desensitization is treatment.

questions.text: Which of the following pair of cell has the ability to produce histamine that mediate inflammation
questions.explanation: Mast cells and basophils release histamine; eosinophils chiefly contain toxic granule proteins and monocytes/B cells do not form this histamine pair.

questions.text: Which of the following cell mediate the hypersensitivity
questions.explanation: Mast cells, basophils and eosinophils all participate in allergic hypersensitivity.

questions.text: A 12 years old boy came to the ER with red swollen face, wheezes and hypotension, his mom said that he had those symptoms after playing with flowers his grandmother brought with from France, his symptoms is mediated by:
options: Liver production of acute phase proteins
questions.explanation: Immediate wheeze, swelling and hypotension follow mast-cell histamine release, unlike delayed acute-phase or eosinophil effects.

questions.text: A 27 year old male patient (blood group O) arrives at the emergency room with massive intestinal bleeding. Within hours he has lost half of his blood volume and blood transfusion is required. Due to human error, blood group AB was transfused to him, and within minutes he develops fever, chills, dyspnea and a dramatic drop in blood pressure. This reaction is most likely due to which of the following?
options: A cell mediated response against AB antigens
IgG production by the recipient in response to AB antigens
Preformed anti-A and anti-B antibodies in the recipient
Preformed anti-A and anti-B antibodies of the blood donor
Preformed isohemagglutinins of the IgG isotype
questions.explanation: Group O recipients carry preformed anti-A and anti-B that attack AB donor erythrocytes.

questions.text: A patient on penicillin developed autoimmune hemolysis which resolved after penicillin withdrawal. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Drug-dependent antibody destruction of erythrocytes is type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity.

questions.text: Of the following four types of hypersensitivity reactions, which one causes the hemolysis that occurs in hemolytic disease of the new born (erythroblastosis fetalis) ?
questions.explanation: Maternal antibodies targeting fetal erythrocytes cause type II hypersensitivity.

questions.text: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia, red blood cells are destructed by :
options: TNF-α are produced by activated macrophages
Immune complexes deposited on RBC membrane
Perforins and granzymes of granules of cytotoxic T cells
Membrane attack complex of activated alternative complement pathway
IgG or IgM against antigen of RBC membrane activating complement forming MAC
questions.explanation: RBC-bound IgG or IgM can activate complement in autoimmune hemolysis.

questions.text: Which of the following is initiated by the interaction of host cell membranes with IgM or IgG antibody but never IgE antibody?
questions.explanation: IgG or IgM on host-cell antigens produces type II hypersensitivity.

questions.text: A 28 year old female presented with an acute urinary tract infection and is given amoxicillin. Her symptoms resolved after completing the course of antibiotic. Two weeks later she presented with fatigue, dyspnea and tachycardia. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is diagnosed base on decreased hemoglobin and a positive direct Coombs test (Presence of antibodies on erythrocyte surface). These findings suggest which type of hypersensitivity?
options: Type I, mediated by CD4+ T cells
Type II mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III mediated by IgM antibodies
Type IV mediated by CD4+ T cells
Type IV mediated by IgE antibodies
questions.explanation: Antibody on erythrocytes causing hemolysis is type II hypersensitivity.

questions.text: A 35 year old male presents with headache, fatigue, difficulty in breathing and rapid heart rate. Lab findings reveal decreased hemoglobin and a positive direct Coomb’s test. The patient is currently taking an antibiotic for symptoms of upper respiratory infection. These findings suggest which type of hypersensitivity?
options: Type I, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type II mediated by Ig G antibodies
Type III mediated by IgG antibodies
Type III mediated by IgG or IgM antibodies
Type IV mediated by CD4 T cells
questions.explanation: A positive direct Coombs test in hemolysis supports type II antibody-mediated injury.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example for cytotoxic hypersensitivity response
questions.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia and rheumatic antibody cross-reactivity are conventionally type II, unlike asthma or poststreptococcal immune-complex GN.

questions.text: An Rh-ve mother is pregnant with an Rh+ve baby. This is her second pregnancy and her first born baby was Rh+ve. Which is the most likely scenario for the outcome of her 2nd baby if there are no medical interventions?
options: The baby will be born healthy
IgM antibodies against Rh will cross the placenta from the mother to the baby causing hemolytic disease of the newborn
IgG antibodies will be transferred from the baby to the mother to destroy her RBC
The baby will develop hemolytic disease of the newborn due to the transfer of IgG antibodies against Rh from the mother across the placenta
questions.explanation: Maternal IgG against Rh crosses the placenta and can hemolyze fetal cells; maternal IgM cannot cross and transfer is not baby-to-mother antibody.

questions.text: A patient was complaining of subcutaneous dark spots, he was diagnosed with thrombocytopenic purpura, which type of HS this disease belongs to?
questions.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia results from antibody-mediated platelet clearance, classified type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity.

questions.text: Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune disease that involves a
questions.explanation: Rheumatic fever conventionally involves cross-reactive antibody against host tissue, a type II mechanism rather than type I or III.

questions.text: The immune pathology relevant to SLE glomerulonephritis is
options: Deposition of circulating immune complexes in glomerular basement membrane followed by activation of complement
Release of histamine and inflammatory mediators from mast cells sensitized by IgE
Destruction of glomerular basement by lysosomal enzymes released from activated macrophages under the effect of IFN-γ released from Th1 cells
Destruction of glomerular basement membrane by proteins and proteolytic enzymes released from eosinophils as major basic protein
Destruction of glomerular basement membrane by cytotoxic cells sensitized against altered self-antigens in the glomerular basement membrane
questions.explanation: Lupus glomerulonephritis is driven by deposited immune complexes and complement.

questions.text: A 77 year old man with enterococcal endocarditis was treated with penicillin G and gentamicin. Five days later fever and a diffuse maculopapular rash developed. There is no urticaria, hypotension, or respiratory compromise. Urine analysis revealed proteinuria and granular casts. You suspect he may have serum sickness. Which one of the following immunopathogenic mechanisms is most likely to be the cause?
options: One of the drugs formed immune complexes with IgG
One of the drugs activated the alternative pathway of complement
One of the drugs activated CD4 positive T cells and macrophages
One of the drugs cross-linked IgE on the mast cells and caused the release of histamine
questions.explanation: Serum sickness is systemic injury from soluble antigen-antibody complexes.

questions.text: A 45 year old female with a history of hepatitis C viral infection presents with decreased renal function, hypertension and anemia/ Lab findings reveal decrease serum C3. Her urine contains leukocytes RBCs, and proteins. These findings suggest which type of hypersensitivity?
options: Type I, mediated by CD4 T cells
Type II, mediated by IgM antibodies
Type III, mediated by IgG antibodies
Type IV, mediated by CD4 T cells
Type IV, mediated by IgG and sometimes IgM antibodies
questions.explanation: Chronic hepatitis with low complement and nephritis suggests immune-complex type III injury.

questions.text: Concerning type 3 HS, which of the following is a clinical presentation
questions.explanation: Serum sickness is systemic immune-complex disease; Goodpasture, Graves and immune cytopenia have type II antibody mechanisms.

questions.text: Which type of cells infiltrated in Arthus reaction?
questions.explanation: Immune-complex complement activation recruits neutrophils; eosinophils, mast cells and basophils emphasize type I allergy.

questions.text: Compare between contact dermatitis and urticaria
questions.modelAnswer: Allergic contact dermatitis is usually type IV hypersensitivity: antigen-specific T cells respond to a skin-contact antigen, and the reaction develops over about 24–72 hours. Classical allergic urticaria is an immediate IgE/mast-cell reaction producing transient itchy wheals through histamine and increased vascular permeability. Urticaria also has non-IgE causes, so the comparison refers to the allergic form.

Urticaria also has non-IgE causes, so the comparison refers to the allergic form.

questions.text: In delayed hypersensitivity skin reactions, which of the following cells is involved in the reaction?
questions.explanation: Delayed-type skin hypersensitivity is mediated by antigen-specific T cells, classically Th1 cytokines that recruit and activate macrophages. Th2 and B-cell responses principally mediate other forms of immunity.

questions.text: In a positive Tuberculin test, which of the following cell surface molecules on APCs is essential for the reaction?
questions.explanation: Tuberculin peptides are presented to CD4 Th1 cells on MHC II.

questions.text: Which of the following cells are involved in granuloma production in patients with tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Th1 cells activate macrophages, which form the granulomatous lesion.

questions.text: A 45 year old man is complaining of weight loss, night sweats and cough of bloody sputum. A PPD skin test is done and the results are positive. What can you conclude from this result?
options: B and T lymphocytes are functional
A humoral immune response has occurred
A cell mediated response has occurred
questions.explanation: A positive PPD records a recall T-cell-mediated inflammatory response.

questions.text: A 25 year old female uses a topical cosmetic cream on her face daily. A week later, presents with an itchy oozing erythematous skin lesion on her face. What do you suspect?
questions.explanation: A rash developing days after cosmetic exposure fits allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.text: Which type of hypersensitivity is associated with reactions to poison ivy oils
questions.explanation: Poison ivy causes a delayed T-cell response.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is characteristic of contact sensitivity?
options: The best therapy is oral administration of the antigen
Patch testing with the allergen is useless for diagnosis
Sensitization can be passively transferred with serum from an allergic individual
Some chemicals acting as hapten induce sensitivity by covalently binding to host proteins acting as carriers
Antihistamines constitute the treatment of choice
questions.explanation: Reactive contact chemicals bind host proteins as haptens and activate T-cell hypersensitivity. Source option b says USELESS, so it is false, rather than another correct diagnosis statement.

questions.text: One important test to determine whether your patient has been exposed to M. tuberculosis, is to do PPD skin test. In this test, PPD extracted from the organism is injected intradermal. Of the following, which one is most likely to occur at the site of a PPD?
options: Cytotoxic T cells kill target cells at the site
Macrophages and CD4 positive T cells infiltrate the area
Histamine and leukotrienes are liberated from mast cells at the site
Immune complexes consisting of PPD are deposited at the site
Plasma cells and sensitized B lymphocytes accumulate at the site
questions.explanation: PPD recruits antigen-specific CD4 Th1 cells and activated macrophages.

questions.text: Of the following diseases, which one is most likely to be caused by a delayed hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell response.

questions.text: In the course of an immune response against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Nonspecific damage is done to previously healthy axons and myelin sheaths. The response involved was most likely .
questions.explanation: Activated Th1/macrophage inflammatory responses can injure nearby normal tissue.

questions.text: A 32 year old farmer has been exposed to poison ivy on several different occasions and he usually gets severe skin lesions. A pharmaceutical company is developing cytokines by recombinant DNA technology and formulating them in a fashion that they are readily absorbed from the skin. Which of the following cytokines administered could inhibit the severity of this reaction?
questions.explanation: IL-10 can suppress experimentally elicited contact hypersensitivity. This is a mechanism question, not established topical human treatment.

questions.text: The following is true regarding type IV hypersensitivity reactions
options: These reactions involve several types of antibodies
They are elicited against parasitic infections
They represent the primary immunopathogenic mechanism in anaphylactic shock
They primarily involve TH1 cells and macrophages
questions.explanation: Delayed type IV responses principally use T cells/macrophages rather than antibodies or anaphylactic IgE mechanisms.

questions.text: A 20 years old female presented with red inflamed skin 2 days after wearing a piece of jewelry, her symptoms are mediated by:
questions.explanation: Jewelry contact dermatitis develops as delayed T-cell immunity; circulating immune complexes or direct C3b excess do not explain the latency.

questions.text: Enumerate three factors contributing to autoimmune disease susceptibility and explain the role of inherited susceptibility.
questions.modelAnswer: Contributors include inherited susceptibility, especially HLA genotype; environmental triggers such as infection and molecular mimicry; and hormonal/sex-related influences. Genetic susceptibility is a major determinant, but no single factor is universally the most important across all autoimmune diseases. Disease emerges from failure of tolerance within a susceptible host.

questions.text: Give 3 examples of Autoimmune diseases addressing the mechanism of tissue damage in each
questions.modelAnswer: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: antibodies coat red cells, promoting Fc-receptor/complement-mediated destruction. Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoantibodies form pathogenic immune complexes that deposit and inflame tissues. Type 1 diabetes mellitus: autoreactive T cells contribute to destruction of pancreatic β cells. These illustrate cell-bound antibody, immune-complex and cellular mechanisms.
points: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: antibodies coat red cells, promoting Fc-receptor/complement-mediated destruction.
Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoantibodies form pathogenic immune complexes that deposit and inflame tissues.
Type 1 diabetes mellitus: autoreactive T cells contribute to destruction of pancreatic β cells.
These illustrate cell-bound antibody, immune-complex and cellular mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia: antibodies coat red cells, promoting Fc-receptor/complement-mediated destruction. Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoantibodies form pathogenic immune complexes that deposit and inflame tissues. questions.text: A 40 year old woman has a history of chronic inflammation of the small joints of hand. A clinician suspects rheumatoid arthritis, which of the following lab findings could confirm his diagnosis?
options: Positive IgM antibody against Fc region of her own IgG
questions.explanation: IgM recognizing the Fc region of IgG is rheumatoid factor.

questions.text: In which of the following autoimmune diseases, An autoantibody against the Fc region of the patient’s own immunoglobulin G is produced and is involved in the pathogenesis of the disease ?
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid factor recognizes the Fc portion of IgG.

questions.text: Cross reacting antibodies against certain M proteins of Strept pyogenes attacking myosin of heart muscle leading to cardiac damage of rheumatic fever is an example of which mechanism of autoimmunity?
questions.explanation: Microbial antigens resembling cardiac antigens cause cross-reactive autoimmunity by molecular mimicry.

questions.text: A 40-year-old woman has a history of chronic inflammation of the small joints of hand, a clinician suspects rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following lab findings could confirm his diagnosis?
options: Positive IgM antibody against Fc region of her own IgG
questions.explanation: IgM antibody against IgG Fc is rheumatoid factor.

questions.text: How can a hapten induce an autoimmune disease?
options: It induces a strong inflammatory response
Acts as a clamp between MHC on antigen presenting cell and β segment of TCR
Acts as a polyclonal B cell activator
Binds to endogenous proteins in host cell forming altered self-antigens
questions.explanation: A hapten binds host proteins to create modified antigens.

questions.text: A defect in which of the following complement components is associated with SLE?
questions.explanation: Early classical complement deficiencies predispose to lupus.

questions.text: A 45 year old female patient suffering from Rheumatoid arthritis is taking an anti- TNF-α monoclonal antibody. The aim of this regimen is to
options: Decrease MHC class II expression on APCs
questions.explanation: TNF blockade reduces the proinflammatory cytokine environment in RA joints.

questions.text: Antibodies against normal components of the body typically occur in autoimmune diseases. In which of the following sets of two diseases do antibodies against DNA occur in one disease and antibodies against IgG occur in the other disease
options: Myasthenia gravis and systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus and Rheumatoid arthritis
questions.explanation: SLE commonly targets nuclear antigens; RA includes anti-IgG rheumatoid factor.

questions.text: An autoimmune disease with shared antigen by the kidney and lung is:
questions.explanation: Goodpasture autoantibodies recognize basement-membrane antigens shared by kidney and lung.

questions.text: A 17 year old boy severely injured his left eye by sharp pieces of glass in a motorcycle accident and the eye was removed. Three weeks later the right eye began to show manifestations of iridocyclitis with photophobia and severe visual impairment. What is the MOST likely immunological basis of this reaction?
options: Alteration of self-antigen by the mechanical damage and becoming immunogenic
Cross reactivity between eye lens and glass
Inherited genetic trait with a strong propensity to develop this reaction
Superantigen effect of glass, leading to massive activation of T-lymphocytes
Visualization of sequestered antigen by autoreactive immune cells
questions.explanation: Eye trauma can expose sequestered ocular antigens and trigger sympathetic ophthalmia.

questions.text: Organ specific autoimmune-diseases include all ofthe following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: SLE is systemic rather than organ-specific.

questions.text: Depressed serum levels of complement could be a sign of:
questions.explanation: Immune complexes activate and consume complement in type III reactions.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an organ specific autoimmune disease?
questions.explanation: RA is conventionally a systemic autoimmune disease.

questions.text: Inactivation or destruction of lymphocytes bearing BCRs or TCRs capable of recognizing and binding specific self-epitopes results in:
questions.explanation: Deletion or inactivation of self-reactive clones establishes self-tolerance.

questions.text: During an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes, an individual generated sufficiently high levels of IgM an IgG antibodies against a S.pyogenes antigen with structural similarity with molecules on the heart that cardiac damage was caused. In this example, the microbe contributed to autoimmunity via a process known as
questions.explanation: Streptococcal antigens resembling cardiac antigens elicit molecular mimicry.

questions.text: In a patient autoimmune type I diabetes mellitus. Destruction of pancreatic β cells occurs by:
questions.explanation: Autoreactive cytotoxic T cells can destroy pancreatic beta cells.

questions.text: In autoimmune type I diabetes mellitus, the immune pathology responsible for destruction is related to
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes beta-cell destruction is principally T-cell mediated.

questions.text: An autoimmune disease which targets nucleic acids is:
questions.explanation: SLE targets ubiquitous nuclear antigens.

questions.text: A 30 year old female presents with fatigue, weight loss. Arthritis of her hands and a malar “butterfly” rash. Blood tests reveal decreased hemoglobin and the presence of antinuclear antibodies. These findings support which of the following diagnoses paired with its underlying immunologic process?
options: Graves’ disease: autoantibodies to thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor
Myasthenia gravis; autoimmunity associated with HLA gene DR3
Reiter syndrome: immune- mediated destruction associated with HLA gene DR4
Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoantibodies to chromosomal proteins
questions.explanation: Malar rash, arthritis and antinuclear antibodies fit SLE targeting nuclear/chromosomal components.

questions.text: A 55 year old female presents with pain and stiffness in her hands and wrists. Lab findings reveal the presence of Rheumatoid factor. Resulting injury that will likely occur in this patient will result from:
options: Both cell mediated and humoral immunity
Both type II and type III hypersensitivity
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis involves T-cell inflammatory pathways and antibody/immune-complex injury. Source b is II plus III, not III plus IV, and therefore does not capture the cellular contribution.

questions.text: All of the following are examples of humoral associated autoimmune diseases EXCEPT:
options: Insulin dependent type I diabetes mellitus
questions.explanation: Insulin-dependent diabetes is principally T-cell-mediated rather than a humoral autoimmune prototype.

questions.text: A 43 year old woman is seen by her physician with complains of painful swollen joints. On examination, her hand appears to be disfigured with subcutaneous nodule formation. Her left knee is markedly enlarged and 100ml of fluid is withdrawn from the joint capsule. An examination of this fluid should reveal which of the following?
options: IgM antibodies reactive against the Fc region of IgG
questions.explanation: RA-associated rheumatoid factor is usually IgM binding IgG Fc.

questions.text: Which of the following is an autoimmune disease?
questions.explanation: SLE targets self antigens; Arthus/contact reactions involve foreign antigen and graft responses recognize alloantigen.

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of an autoimmune disease caused by type IV
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis includes T-cell-mediated autoimmunity; contact dermatitis and farmer's lung are not autoimmune despite hypersensitivity.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT an autoimmune disease:
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis targets exogenous contact allergens; Graves, MS, RA and SLE target self.

questions.text: Molecular mimicry is a mechanism that can potentially trigger an autoimmune disease. This is because:
options: Viruses and bacteria have antigenic determinants that are similar to human antigens
T cell receptors can change their antigen specificity to become autoimmune
This process results interferes with central tolerance mechanisms
Mimicry involves abnormal signaling in T cells which triggers autoimmune diseases
Pathogens can cause a change in the specificity of T cell receptors
questions.explanation: Microbial/self determinant similarity allows cross-reactivity; TCR specificity does not change to create molecular mimicry.

questions.text: Ag cross reaction can trigger autoimmune disease because of
options: TCR change their antigens specificity to become self reactive
Some viruses and bacteria have Ag determinants similar to human antigens
questions.explanation: Molecular mimicry involves microbial determinants resembling host antigens, rather than changing TCR gene specificity.

questions.text: Enumerate three central-tolerance mechanisms during lymphocyte maturation.
questions.modelAnswer: During central lymphocyte maturation, strongly self-reactive cells may be removed by clonal deletion. Immature B cells may alter their receptor specificity through receptor editing. Some self-reactive CD4 T cells differentiate into thymic regulatory T cells that help maintain tolerance. These mechanisms begin during development and continue after birth; they are not confined to intrauterine life.

Immature B cells may alter their receptor specificity through receptor editing.
Some self-reactive CD4 T cells differentiate into thymic regulatory T cells that help maintain tolerance.

questions.text: Enumerate 3 mechanisms of tolerance in periphral tisuse
questions.modelAnswer: Peripheral tolerance includes anergy when antigen is recognized without adequate co-stimulation; deletion of activated/self-reactive cells by apoptosis; and suppression by regulatory T cells, including inhibitory cytokines and restriction of APC/T-cell activation.
points: Peripheral tolerance includes anergy when antigen is recognized without adequate co-stimulation; deletion of activated/self-reactive cells by apoptosis; and suppression by regulatory T cells, including inhibitory cytokines and restriction of APC/T-cell activation.
questions.explanation: Peripheral tolerance includes anergy when antigen is recognized without adequate co-stimulation; deletion of activated/self-reactive cells by apoptosis; and suppression by regulatory T cells, including inhibitory cytokines and restriction of APC/T-cell activation.

questions.text: Compare between intrinsic and extrinsic pathway of deletion
questions.modelAnswer: Intrinsic deletion uses mitochondrial apoptosis, regulated by BCL-2-family proteins: cytochrome c release activates the apoptosome/caspase-9 pathway. Extrinsic deletion begins at death receptors such as Fas when Fas ligand binds, activating caspase-8. Both pathways converge on executioner caspases and apoptotic removal of the lymphocyte.

questions.text: Discuss how T-regulatory play an important role in prevention of Autoimmune disorders
questions.modelAnswer: FOXP3-positive regulatory T cells restrain activation, proliferation and cytokine production of other lymphocytes. They can release inhibitory mediators such as IL-10 and TGF-β and use regulatory receptor pathways including CTLA-4. Their control of self-reactive responses prevents inappropriate tissue injury; defective FOXP3 regulation causes severe autoimmunity in IPEX.

questions.text: If a patient with an autoimmune disease develops T cells with T cell receptors specific to self-antigens, failure of which process leads to this result?
questions.explanation: Negative selection eliminates strongly self-reactive developing T cells.

questions.text: What is the fate of T cells stimulated by a peptide /MHC complex displayed on antigen presenting cells in the absence of costimulation?
questions.explanation: Antigen recognition without costimulation can induce anergy or deletion.

questions.text: The most probable fate of an autoreactive T cell that has escaped central tolerance is:
options: Recognition of self-antigen ,then activation and proliferation into a clone
Deletion by apoptosis by peripheral tolerance mechanisms
Uncontrolled rapid division triggering a cancer
questions.explanation: Peripheral deletion is a protective fate of escaped autoreactive clones.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a peripheral tolerance mechanism?
options: Deletion by apoptosis caused by repeated activation of self-reactive cells
Loss of T cell help needed for self-reactive B cells
questions.explanation: Receptor editing is principally an immature B-cell central tolerance mechanism.

questions.text: A soluble free epitope is recognized by the B cell receptor on a circulating b cell. No additional stimulation is provided by a CD4+ t cell. Such a B cell
options: Will be engulfed by a macrophage
questions.explanation: Antigen recognition without required T-cell help can render a B cell unresponsive.

questions.text: A state of T- lymphocyte non responsiveness that occurs following peptide + MHC engagement is known as
questions.explanation: Anergy is antigen-specific functional unresponsiveness.

questions.text: The term tolerance refers to:
options: PAMP recognition by pattern recognition receptors
Restriction of CD4 T cells to MHC class II molecules
Selective unresponsiveness of T cells to certain antigens
T cell recognition of soluble molecules
The interface between APCs and T cells
questions.explanation: Tolerance is antigen-specific immune unresponsiveness.

questions.text: A 45 year old female patient suffering from Rheumatoid arthritis is taking an anti- TNF-α monoclonal antibody. The aim of this regimen is to elevate:
questions.explanation: Infliximab can restore/induce regulatory T-cell populations in RA.

questions.text: In a successful treatment regimen of Rheumatoid arthritis. T regulatory cells were elevated. Which of the following cytokines is expected to be elevated:
questions.explanation: Treatment-associated suppressive Tregs can act through IL-10 and TGF-beta.

questions.text: The failure to inactivate or eliminate self-reactive cells results in
questions.explanation: Failure of self-reactive-cell control enables autoimmunity.

questions.text: Failure of the immune system to respond against a self-epitope in an strong way is termed;
questions.explanation: Tolerance describes the absence of an immune response to specific antigens.

questions.text: A 50 year old female suffering from rheumatoid arthritis started to take infliximab (anti-TNF-α). This therapy increased the production of CD25+ T cells. Which of the following is likely to become elevated in this patient?
questions.explanation: Infliximab-associated suppressive Tregs can mediate regulation through IL-10.

questions.text: Why an individual normally does not make an immune response to a self-protein?
options: Self-proteins cannot be processed into peptides
Lymphocytes that express a receptor reactive to a self-protein are inactivated by deletion, anergy, or receptor editing
Peptides from self-proteins cannot bind to MHC class I molecules
Peptides from self-proteins cannot bind to MHC class II molecules
questions.explanation: Self-reactive lymphocytes are eliminated, edited or silenced; self peptides can be processed and loaded onto either MHC class.

questions.text: In which of the following organs does central tolerance occur?
questions.explanation: Thymus is a primary lymphoid site of central T-cell tolerance; marrow is the B-cell site and is not offered.

questions.text: Receptor editing is
options: A method by which antibodies cross react to cause autoimmune diseases
The mechanism by which superantigens can cause activation of T cell receptors of variable specificities
A mechanism by which T cells change their antigen receptors after encountering an antigen in the periphery in adult patients with autoimmune disease
questions.explanation: Immature B-cell receptor editing in marrow supports central tolerance; mature TCR switching and superantigen activation are different claims.

questions.text: Anergy is best defined as
options: A growth arrest state that occurs when a T cell is activated in the absence of costimulation
A method of central tolerance where autoreactive T cells are deleted in fetal life
A method of ensuring that autoreactive cells are deleted by activation induced cell death
questions.explanation: Anergy is functional nonresponse after inadequate costimulation, rather than deletion or apoptosis.

questions.text: The following is a mechanism of central tolerance ONLY:
questions.explanation: Receptor editing is the classic central immature-B-cell mechanism; Treg development can be peripheral and apoptosis occurs in both settings.

questions.text: An autograft of a burn victim is best described by which one of the following?
options: Transplant from one region of a person to another region
Transplant from one person to a genetically identical person
Transplant from one species to the same species
Transplant from one species to another species
questions.explanation: An autograft transfers tissue within the same individual.

questions.text: A 21 year old patient in severe kidney failure receives a kidney from his 30 year old brother. This type of transplantation is best described by which of the following?
options: Allograft: transplant from one species to the same species
Autograft: transplant from one region of a person to another region
Isograft: transplant from one person to a genetically identical person
Xenograft: transplant from one species to another species
questions.explanation: A kidney transferred between ordinary brothers is an allograft.

questions.text: A 32-year-old male receives a kidney transplant from female donor. Once the kidney is anatomized to the man’s vasculature, the transplant team immediately begins to observe swelling and interstitial hemorrhage. After the surgery, the patient developed fever and leukocytosis and produced no urine. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Acute rejection due to antibody-mediated immunity
Acute rejection due to cell-mediated immunity
Chronic rejection due to cell-mediated immunity to minor HLA antigens
Hyperacute rejection due to lymphocyte and macrophage infiltration
Hyperacute rejection due to preformed antibodies
questions.explanation: Rejection immediately after vascular connection indicates preformed antibody.

questions.text: Which of the following statements concerning hyperacute graft rejection is true?
options: It is mediated by activated T-lymphocytes
Can be prevented by cross-match test
Can be controlled by increased immunosuppressive therapy
questions.explanation: Pretransplant antibody crossmatching detects incompatibility underlying hyperacute rejection.

questions.text: A graft that transfers tissues or an organ from one member of a species to a member of another species is called:
questions.explanation: Different-species transplantation is a xenograft.

questions.text: A graft transferred between two identical twins is:
questions.explanation: Genetically identical twins supply syngeneic/isografts.

questions.text: A 47 year old male has a history of end stage renal failure and required a kidney transplant. Approximately 4 weeks after receiving his transplanted kidney, he developed oliguria (decreased production of urine), fever, hypertension, and pain or tenderness over the allograft. On the basis of these findings, the most likely underlying immunological process is:
questions.explanation: Tender graft dysfunction several weeks after transplantation fits acute rejection.

questions.text: What is a graft between different members of the same species termed?
questions.explanation: An allograft is between genetically different members of one species; autograft is self, isograft genetically identical and xenograft cross-species.

questions.text: In clinical transplantation, preformed cytotoxic antibodies reactive against antigens expressed on the grafted tissue:
options: Activate cytotoxic T cells, which then cause hyperacute rejection
Binds to antigens in graft vascular endothelium leading to hyperacute rejection
Cause delayed rejection of the transplant
Activate macrophages, which then present the graft antigens to helper T cells
questions.explanation: Preformed antibodies bind graft vascular endothelium and trigger hyperacute rejection, not a delayed T-cell reaction.

questions.text: Which of the following problems can occur by the recipient preformed cytotoxic antibodies which react against MHC antigens expressed on the grafted tissue?
questions.explanation: Preformed donor-reactive antibody produces hyperacute rejection; GVHD is donor lymphocyte attack and chronic/acute cellular rejection have other timing.

questions.text: Which of the following allogenic grafts does not require immune suppression
questions.explanation: Avascular corneal grafts commonly survive without systemic immunosuppression, unlike marrow, heart or pancreatic grafts.

questions.text: HLA cross match is one of the tests performed prior to organ transplantation. A +ve cross match means:
options: The donor is a good match
Recipient has preformed Abs against donor's lymphocytes
It's likely that recipient will face chronic rejection
Recipient lymphocytes will lyse donor's lymphocytes
questions.explanation: Positive crossmatch indicates recipient antibody against donor leukocytes; it predicts hyperacute risk rather than a good match or chronic rejection alone.

questions.text: Which one of the following is the BEST method of reducing Graft-versus host reaction in a bone marrow recipient:
options: Matching the complement components of donor and recipient
Removing mature T cells from the graft
Removing mature B cells from the graft
Removing Pre-B cells from the graft
questions.explanation: Removing mature donor T cells reduces graft-versus-host reactions.

questions.text: The immunosuppressive effect of Cyclosporine A is due to its ability to :
questions.explanation: Cyclosporin inhibits calcineurin-dependent IL-2 transcription in activated T cells.

questions.text: Transplantation involving tissue from two brothers possessing the same identical HLA genes is best described by which one of the following?
options: Allograft: transplant from one species to the same species
Autograft: transplant from one region of a person to another region
Isograft: transplant from one person to a genetically identical person
Xenograft: transplant from one species to another species
questions.explanation: HLA-identical brothers remain allogeneic unless genetically identical twins; matching HLA alone does not make an isograft.

questions.text: An 18 year old male patient with acute lymphocytic leukemia is prepared for bone marrow transplantation from an HLA non identical donor. Prior to the transplantation broad spectrum antibiotics and an immunosuppressive regimen was given. Within 2 to 4 weeks, lymphocyte and granulocyte numbers begin to rise confirming bone marrow engraftment. However one month later, the patient develops diarrhea, jaundice and a severe maculopapular rash. Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. Which of the following is most likely occurring?
questions.explanation: Donor lymphocytes after marrow transplantation can injure skin, liver and gut.

questions.text: A 6 year old male receives a bone marrow transplant from his father during treatment of acute myeloid leukemia. What is the most likely threat to occur?
questions.explanation: Allogeneic marrow contains mature donor T cells capable of causing GVHD.

questions.text: After receiving a kidney transplant from the most appropriate donor, a 38 year old female was put on cyclosporine as a part of an immunosuppressive regimen. How does this drug act?
options: Decrease antibody secretion by plasma cells
Decrease T cell production of IL-2
Suppress alternative pathway of complement activation
questions.explanation: Cyclosporin suppresses IL-2 production and T-cell proliferation.

questions.text: Regarding Graft versus host reaction, which one of the following is MOST accurate?
options: It occurs primarily when a kidney is transplanted
It occurs primarily by mature T cells in a bone marrow transplant
It occurs when ABO blood groups are not matched
It occurs when the donor is immunocompromised
It occurs when haplotypes of donor and recipient are identical
questions.explanation: GVHD is caused by mature donor T cells, particularly after marrow transplantation.

questions.text: Immunosuppressive drugs administered after transplantation greatly enhance the recipient’s susceptibility to:
questions.explanation: Immunosuppression increases opportunistic infection and neoplasia risks.

questions.text: Glucocorticoids exert immunosuppressive effects by:
options: Binding to intracellular receptors and influencing gene transcription of cytokines
Impairing the ability of platelets to aggregate
Stimulating IL-2 production and T cell proliferation
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids bind intracellular receptors that alter cytokine gene transcription.

questions.text: After receiving a kidney transplant from the most appropriate available donor, a 38 year old female is administered immunosuppressive drugs, including cyclosporine in order to
options: Decrease T cell production of IL-2
Destroy stem cells in her bone marrow
Reduce plasma cell secretion of IgG antibodies
questions.explanation: Calcineurin blockade reduces T-cell IL-2 transcription.

questions.text: In heart-lung transplantation, patients are treated with anti CD28 antibody fragment at the time of transplantation and at monthly intervals thereafter. What would be the goal of such therapy?
options: To induce anergy to transplanted tissues
To inhibit mitosis in B cells
To inhibit mitosis in T cells
questions.explanation: Blocking CD28 costimulation during antigen recognition can induce T-cell anergy.

questions.text: An 11 year old male with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receives a bone marrow transplant from his older sister that contains stem cells and mature T cells. Development of which of the following will be of primary concern in this patient?
questions.explanation: Mature donor T cells can attack recipient tissue after marrow transplantation.

questions.text: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia is under irradiation and chemotherapy., while awaiting bone marrow transplantation from a closely matched sibling. Six months after the transplant symptoms of generalized skin rash with desquamation, jaundice and bloody diarrhea begin to appear. What is the immunological effector mechanism most closely associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Donor cytotoxic T cells cause epithelial injury in GVHD.

questions.text: A 1 yo boy with acute lymphoblastic leukemia receives a bone marrow transplantation from his older sister. That contains stem cells and mature T cells, which of the following disorders is more likely to occur in his case:
questions.explanation: Mature donor T cells in marrow graft can attack recipient tissue, causing GVHD; the other options concern host rejection or unrelated hypersensitivity.

questions.text: Decrease expression of MHC class I on tumor cells will impair the activity of .......... cell, on the other hand it will enhance recognition by ............
options: T cytotoxic T cell/ NK cell
questions.explanation: Loss of tumor MHC I impairs CTL recognition but can release NK inhibition.

questions.text: What is the most important cell in anti-tumor immunity?
questions.explanation: Tumor-specific cytotoxic T cells are principal adaptive antitumor effectors.

questions.text: Regarding tumor immunity, which one of the following is MOST accurate?
options: Both cytotoxic T cells and cytotoxic antibodies attack cancer cells
An elevated level of α-fetoprotein is a marker for lung carcinoma
A declining level of carcinoembryonic antigen is an indication of recurrence of colon cancer
Cancer cells induced by chemicals have new antigens, but those induced by viruses do not
NK cells don’t participate in immune response to cancer cells as they lack antigen receptors
questions.explanation: Both cytotoxic T cells and antibody-directed mechanisms can attack cancer cells.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is CORRECT as regards tumor specific antigens
options: Their expression results in apoptosis of tumor cells
They are normal cellular proteins expressed in fetal life, but are lost during adult life
They may be mutant cellular oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes, or antigens of oncogenic viruses expressed only on tumor cells
They are sequestered antigens e.g. eye lens, sperms and CNS which have no access to the immune system
They are identified on most naturally occurring tumors
questions.explanation: Mutated cellular proteins and viral oncogenic proteins can yield tumor-specific antigens.

questions.text: According to immune surveillance theory, which of the following statements is CORRECT?
options: Antibodies arise during fetal development that can destroy tumors
Cancer cells rarely arise within a normal individual
Innate immune responses eliminate specific tumor cell antigens
Tumors arise only if malignant cells escape immune detection
Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes prevent malignant transformations
questions.explanation: Immune surveillance theory proposes removal of transformed cells unless they escape detection.

questions.text: Loss of which of the following molecules on the tumor cell surface would result in recognition and killing by Natural killer cells:
questions.explanation: MHC I loss removes inhibitory signals from NK cells.

questions.text: The normal immunological control of tumors is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Immune surveillance denotes physiologic immune monitoring of tumors; anergy, tolerance and escape describe failure or suppression.

questions.text: Which of the following immunotherapeutic approaches in treating tumors is defined as checkpoint blockade?
options: Injecting antibodies conjugated to toxic drugs
Use of lymphokine activated killer cells
Injecting antibodies against PD-1 or its ligand PD-L1
questions.explanation: Anti-PD1/PDL1 blocks inhibitory checkpoint signaling; toxin conjugates, vaccines and cell transfers use different strategies.

questions.text: Which of the following is considered passive immunotherapy for cancer
options: Injection of substances that induce inflammatory response
Injection of tumor cells that is transfected with B7 gene
questions.explanation: Administered monoclonal antibody supplies an effector directly, unlike vaccination, inflammatory stimulation or engineered tumor-cell immunization.

questions.text: Tumor cells may escape immunosurveillance by which of the following mechanisms
options: Expression of high levels of MHC-I molecules
Expression of high levels of B7 molecules
Expression of high levels of PD-L1
questions.explanation: Tumor PD-L1 inhibits PD-1 T cells; increased antigen/MHC-I/B7 generally aids recognition or activation.

questions.text: A cytokine with a known anti-tumor activity is;
questions.explanation: IFN-gamma promotes cellular anti-tumor effector functions and antigen presentation.

questions.text: Lymphokine activated killer cells are:
options: Malignant cells transfected with the costimulatory molecule B7
Monocytes grown in the presence of IFN-γ to increase expression of MHC
B lymphocytes grown in the presence of IL-6 to enhance antibody production
NK cells cultivated in vitro in the presence of high conc. of IL-2
Cytotoxic T cell cultured in the presence of TNF-α to increase its killing effect
questions.explanation: High-dose IL-2 activates cytotoxic lymphocytes including NK cells into LAK populations.

questions.text: In trial to augment the immune response of T lymphocytes against malignant cells in a melanoma patient. Melanoma cells were induced to express costimulatory molecules by transfection. Which of the following molecules would be the best candidate for transfection of tumor cells to achieve this goal?
questions.explanation: B7 on tumor cells supplies costimulation for T-cell priming.

questions.text: A patient with a solid malignant tumor whose cells don’t express MHC class I antigen. Which of the following in vitro treatments of his tumor cells is most likely to stimulate the most effective immune response when reinfused into the patient?
questions.explanation: Interferons enhance MHC expression and recognition by cytotoxic T cells.

questions.text: In a woman with advanced metastatic breast cancer, a bone marrow aspirate was treated with GM-CSF, TNF-α and IL-2 then pulsed with membrane fragments of her tumor cells and reinfused .Which of the following cell subpopulations is the most directly targeted by this treatment?
questions.explanation: Antigen-pulsed marrow-derived dendritic cells prime tumor-specific CTLs.

questions.text: In tumor immunotherapy; which of the following enhances ACTIVE immune response against tumors?
options: Tumor modified cells or purified antigens
questions.explanation: Tumor vaccines induce the recipient’s own antigen-specific response.

questions.text: A 6 year old African boy is admitted to an oncology center for treatment of an advanced case of Burkitt lymphoma. Analysis of malignant cells revealed that they are lacking MHC class I antigens. Which of the following cytokines produced by recombinant DNA technology could be injected into his solid tumor to increase the tumor’s cell susceptibility to CD8 mediated killing?
questions.explanation: IFN-gamma enhances MHC I expression and tumor peptide display to CD8 cells.

subjects.name: Microbiology
subjects.lectures: Antibody and combined immunodeficiencies, Complement deficiency and angioedema, Phagocyte defects, Secondary immunodeficiency and HIV

questions.text: A young patient with severe recurrent Pyogenic bacterial infection, but with normal T cell and B cell numbers. Lab testing reveals that CD4 T helper cells have a defective CD40L molecule. As a result Humoral immunity reveals a significant elevation in which of the following immunoglobulins? What is the cause?
options: IgA/ due to recurrent mucosal infections
IgM/ due to defective isotype switching
IgG/ due to secondary immune response by the recurrent pyogenic infections
IgD/ due to defective CD4 helper function
IgE/ due to allergic response to certain proteins of pyogenic bacteria
questions.explanation: Defective CD40L impairs T-dependent class switching, leaving IgM normal/elevated and IgG/IgA/IgE low despite preserved B-cell numbers.

questions.text: Which of the following immunological procedures would be the BEST to determine the number of CD4+ cells in a patient with HIV?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry counts immunophenotyped CD4-positive lymphocytes.

questions.text: A newborn is evaluated for immunologic function. He has a fish mouth and low set, malformed ears and widely spaced eyes, X-ray finding show cardiac malformation and absence of Thymic shadow. Which of the following parameters would be normal in this child?
options: Cytotoxic killing of virus infected targets
Generation of oxygen metabolites in phagocytic cells
Delayed type hypersensitivity in response to tuberculin
Production of IFN-γ from T helper 1 cells
questions.explanation: DiGeorge impairs thymic T-cell development while phagocyte oxidative metabolism is preserved.

questions.text: A 14 month old male infant is suffering from repeated attacks of otitis media, sinusitis and pneumonia. Moreover, attempts to induce immunity using the Pneumococcal vaccine have failed. Lab findings reveal absence of B lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Absent B cells with recurrent bacterial infections indicates XLA.

questions.text: A 10 month old male infant with recurrent H. influenza infections presents to the emergency room with otitis media, sinusitis, and in severe respiratory distress. Immunological and genetic testing reveals absence of b cells and a destructive mutation in the tyrosine kinase gene. This X-linked recessive immune disorder is usually associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: BTK deficiency prevents mature B-cell development with relatively preserved T-cell function.

questions.text: Amniocentesis was done during genetic counseling of a pregnant woman reveals a fetal adenosine deaminase deficiency. This autosomal recessive immunodeficiency is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: ADA deficiency causes SCID affecting cellular and humoral adaptive responses.

questions.text: An 8 month old male infant has a history of chronic diarrhea, otitis media and several attacks of pneumonia is presented to the pediatric clinician with gingivostomatitis and oral thrush (candida). X-ray and lab testing reveals: absence of thymic shadow and absence of B lymphocytes. History taken from the mother reveals a rash evident at birth. Which of the following diseases is MOST likely present in this infant?
questions.explanation: Absent thymic shadow and B cells with broad opportunistic infections indicates combined deficiency.

questions.text:
Case context: An 8 month old male infant has a history of chronic diarrhea, otitis media and several attacks of pneumonia is presented to the pediatric clinician with gingivostomatitis and oral thrush (candida). X-ray and lab testing reveals: absence of thymic shadow and absence of B lymphocytes. History taken from the mother reveals a rash evident at birth. Which of the following diseases is MOST likely present in this infant?

For this case, which of the following is the best therapy for the infant?
questions.explanation: SCID can be corrected by hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation.

questions.text: A 9 month old infant presents with otitis media and upper respiratory infection. Two months later he is admitted to hospital due to pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. After several more episodes of bacterial infection his doctor recommended various lab tests which revealed normal complement levels, normal neutrophil numbers, positive tuberculin test, but depressed levels of all immunoglobulin classes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Absent antibodies with intact tuberculin reactivity supports a primary B-cell defect.

questions.text: Which of the following microbe infections are more common in patients with Bruton’s agammaglobulinaemia?
questions.explanation: H influenzae is a common encapsulated bacterial pathogen in XLA.

questions.text: A young girl with repeated infections with Candida albicans and respiratory viruses since she was 3 months. If an immune deficiency disease is suspected. Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated
questions.explanation: Severe T-cell defects make live attenuated vaccines unsafe.

questions.text: An individual is given therapy with human immunoglobulin (HIg). Which of the following conditions would be appropriate for this type of therapy?
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin replacement treats deficient antibody production in XLA.

questions.text: An immune deficiency disease characterized by defective cell mediated immunity, hypocalcemia and tetany is;
questions.explanation: Thymic hypoplasia with parathyroid deficiency explains T-cell impairment and hypocalcemic tetany.

questions.text: In X- linked hyper IgM syndrome, What is the affected gene responsible for the immunodeficiency and in which cells?
questions.explanation: X-linked hyper-IgM results from CD40LG dysfunction in activated helper T cells.

questions.text: A patient with X-linked hyper IgM syndrome has an increased susceptibility to:
questions.explanation: CD40L deficiency affects antibody switching and cellular antimicrobial responses.

questions.text: Which of the following is the most common to be deficient in a patient with congenital recurrent respiratory infection and diarrhea?
questions.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency is the commonest inherited immunoglobulin deficiency.

questions.text: A 37 year old male presents for evaluation if recurrent sinus infections requiring antibiotic treatment. He had a history of bacterial pneumonia and chronic diarrhea. Lab testing reveals decreased levels of serum IgG and mildly decreased levels of IgA. The disorder most likely to be responsible for the findings in this patient is:
questions.explanation: Adult recurrent sinopulmonary infections with low IgG/IgA fit CVID.

questions.text: An individual is given therapy with human immune globulin. Which of the following conditions would be appropriate for this type of therapy?
questions.explanation: Pooled immunoglobulin replaces absent circulating antibody.

questions.text: A 5 year old girl has a small deletion in chromosome 22. She has impaired Thymic development with a significant deficiency in the number of functional T cells. The most likely etiology for these findings is
questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion causes abnormal thymic development in DiGeorge syndrome.

questions.text: An 8 year old boy suffers from recurrent bacterial infections including many episodes of pneumococcal sepsis. When he was vaccinated by pneumococcal vaccine he didn’t produce any antibodies to the antigen in the vaccine. What is impaired in this situation
options: Formation of the membrane attack complex
IFN-γ secretion by CD4+ T cells
T cell precursor migration to the thymus
questions.explanation: Failure to generate vaccine antibody impairs antibody-mediated bacterial clearance.

questions.text: An 8 year old boy suffers from recurrent bacterial infections including many episodes of pneumococcal sepsis. When he was vaccinated by pneumococcal vaccine he didn’t produce any antibodies to the antigen in the vaccine. These findings support the diagnosis of :
questions.explanation: Recurrent pneumococcal disease and failure to form vaccine antibody fit XLA.

questions.text: A 6 month old male infant has diarrhea, extensive fungal infections, and skin rashes and has failed to gain weight. The thymus is of normal size. The most likely prospect for permanent restoration of normal immunity for this patient would be
options: An antibiotic cocktail given at regular intervals
Thymic hormones given throughout his life
questions.explanation: A severe combined immune defect requires hematopoietic immune reconstitution.

questions.text: A female neonate has a malformed jaw, cardiac abnormalities, and hypocalcemia, in addition to diminished cell-mediated and B-cell responses. Which of the following immune deficiencies should be included in the differential diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation: Cardiac anomalies, jaw malformation, hypocalcemia and cellular deficiency indicate DiGeorge.

questions.text: A neonatal female child is evaluated for malformation of the face and jaw. Additional testing reveals a small deletion in chromosome 22 as well as abnormalities of the aorta and parathyroid gland. The most likely consequence of her condition will be an impairment of
questions.explanation: 22q11.2 deletion with parathyroid defects points to thymic T-cell impairment.

questions.text: A mother of a 2 yo boy came to the pediatric clinic complaining that her son has recurrent pyogenic infections, investigations revealed decreased levels of immunoglobulin and B cells, his diagnosis is most probably:
questions.explanation: Low circulating B cells and immunoglobulins in a boy with pyogenic infections suggests BTK-related XLA; hyper-IgM retains B cells.

questions.text: Your patient is a 20- year old woman who complains of swelling on her arms and legs and a feeling of fullness in her throat that makes it difficult to breath. The swellings are not red, hot, or tender. You suspect she may have an angioedema caused by a complement abnormality. Of the following, which one is the most likely explanation?
options: She has deficiency in C1 inhibitor
She has a deficiency in C3b
She has a deficiency in factor B
questions.explanation: Nonurticarial swelling with throat/abdominal involvement suggests C1-inhibitor-related bradykinin angioedema rather than excess C9/C5a or C3/factorB deficiency.

questions.text: A patient has been hospitalized three times for painful abdominal edema and is complaining now of swollen lip. What laboratory finding in this patient is expected?
options: Abnormal superoxide anion production by neutrophils
questions.explanation: C1-inhibitor deficiency can produce recurrent abdominal/lip swelling with low C4; phagocyte/T-cell defects fit different syndromes.

questions.text: A 2 year old boy suffering from repeated painful bouts of inflammation of mucosal surfaces, especially affecting the lips, is brought to the pediatrician’s office. His mother gives a positive family history of similar conditions and fears food allergy. What laboratory finding would best support the physician’s suspicion?
questions.explanation: C1-inhibitor-associated hereditary angioedema typically consumes C4.

questions.text: A 30 year old male presents to the emergency room with difficulty in breathing and abdominal pain. On examination edema of his face especially the perioral and periorbital areas was detected together with swelling in the mouth, pharynx and larynx. No pruritus. Lab testing reveals a complement problem. Which of the following is most likely?
options: High C1 esterase inhibitor and low C4
Low C1 esterase inhibitor and low C4
Low C1 esterase inhibitor and high C4
questions.explanation: Nonpruritic airway and abdominal swelling fits C1-inhibitor-deficient hereditary angioedema.

questions.text: A 16 year old female patient is evaluated for a history of frequent, severe abdominal pain. Imaging studies do not reveal a cause of her pain, Further questioning reveals a history of swelling of the face and an episode that involved difficulty in swallowing and swelling of her throat that was assumed but be allergic in nature. The disorder most likely to be responsible for the findings in this patient is:
questions.explanation: Recurrent unexplained abdominal pain and episodic facial/airway swelling fits hereditary angioedema.

questions.text: Genetic deficiency of which of the following is associated with hereditary angioedema?
questions.explanation: C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema; C3/MAC defects cause different infection risks and factor H regulates alternative complement.

questions.text: What is the immune defect in patients with chronic granulomatous disease ?
options: Inability of phagocytic cells to ingest pathogens
Decreased motility and chemotaxis of phagocytic cells
Inability of phagocytic cells to kill ingested pathogens
Defective cell mediated immunity leading to granuloma formation
Decreased level of adhesion molecule expression on phagocytic cells
questions.explanation: NADPH oxidase dysfunction impairs killing after phagocytosis.

questions.text: A two year old who is suffering from recurrent bacterial infections is evaluated for immunological deficiency. The child has normal numbers of CD19 and CD3 cell but has high levels of neutrophils (neutrophilia). The nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction test is normal. What immune defect and disease is expected ?
options: Absence of C1 inhibitor / Hereditary angioneurotic edema
Absence of CD18 (beta subunit of Integrin)/ Leukocyte adhesion deficiency
Absence of DAF / Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
Absence of adenosine deaminase enzyme/ SCID
Deficiency of CD40L/ Hyperlinked IgM syndrome
questions.explanation: CD18 deficiency prevents neutrophil extravasation, producing circulating neutrophilia with normal oxidative burst.

questions.text: A 4 year old boy presents with a severe Staphylococcus aureus abscess. His history is positive for infection with catalase positive bacteria. If he has an enzyme deficiency, which of the following is most likely?
questions.explanation: Catalase-positive infections and abscesses suggest defective NADPH oxidase.

questions.text: A year old baby is brought by his mother to a pediatric clinic due to several boil like lesions on his arm. His mother told the doctor that he had repeated lesions on several different occasions. Antibiotic were prescribed and lesions resolved but multiple investigations were required due to suspected immunodeficiency by the doctor. His investigations revealed normal immunoglobulin levels, normal B and T cell counts, normal complement levels, normal Ca and parathyroid hormone levels and a negative nitroblue tetrazolium test. Which disease is indicated by these findings?
questions.explanation: A negative NBT reduction test indicates impaired phagocyte oxidative burst.

questions.text: The immunological defect in Chediak Higashi syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Chediak-Higashi disrupts lysosomal trafficking and phagolysosomal function.

questions.text: An 8 month old female patient is evaluated for recurrent bacterial infections. Examination reveals albinism of the eyes and skin. Testing reveals decreased NK and T cells functions and impaired fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes. The disorder most likely to be responsible for the findings in this patient is:
questions.explanation: Albinism and phagolysosomal/cytotoxic defects are characteristic of Chediak-Higashi.

questions.text: Which one of the following factors characterizes the immune deficiency in chronic granulomatous disease?
options: Inability of polymorphonuclear leukocytes to kill ingested bacteria
Inability of polymorphonuclear leukocytes to ingest bacteria
Reduced levels of the third component of complement (C3)
questions.explanation: CGD impairs oxidative killing after ingestion; it does not chiefly prevent ingestion, antibodies, C3 or common γ-chain signaling.

questions.text: An 18 year old male heroin addict, who practices the sharing of needles, is positive for the screening test for AIDS. This patient is most likely to be immunodeficient because of which one of the following?
options: A low helper T lymphocyte count
questions.explanation: HIV progressively depletes CD4 helper T cells.

questions.text: Nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction test is used for assay of which of the following?
questions.explanation: NBT evaluates the neutrophil oxidative burst contributing to microbial killing.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of secondary immunodeficiency?
questions.explanation: CLL is an acquired cause of antibody deficiency.

questions.text: All of the following lead to secondary immunodeficiency EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: CGD is inherited, whereas the other choices are acquired causes.

questions.text: A 24 year old male. presents with fever, cough and night sweats. Examination reveals an elevated temperature, increased respiratory rate, oral thrush. lab findings reveal a CD4 count of 60/ml. On the basis of these findings, the most likely underlying process is
questions.explanation: Profound CD4 depletion with oral thrush suggests AIDS and possible opportunistic tuberculosis.

questions.text: A 31-year-old man with AIDS complains of difficulty swallowing. Examination of his oral cavity demonstrated whitish membranes covering much of his tongue and palate. Endoscopy also reveals several whitish, ulcerated lesions in the esophagus. These pathologic findings are fundamentally caused by loss of which of the following immune cells in this patient?
questions.explanation: HIV depletes CD4 helper cells and permits opportunistic Candida, not chiefly B, NK or monocyte depletion.

questions.text: A major factor in promoting the killing of intracellular bacteria by macrophages is:
questions.explanation: IFN-γ activates macrophages for intracellular killing; IL-1/6 are inflammatory and type I IFN antiviral.

questions.text: In clinical transplantation, what is the type of immune rejection in case of presence of recipient cytotoxic antibodies reactive against antigens expressed on the grafted tissue?
options: Cause delayed rejection of the transplant
Binds to antigens in graft vascular endothelium leading to hyperacute rejection
Are not usually directed against HLA antigens
Activate macrophages, which then present the graft antigens to helper T cells
Activate cytotoxic T cells, which then cause hyperacute rejection
questions.explanation: Preformed donor-reactive antibody injures graft endothelium and causes hyperacute rejection rather than delayed cellular rejection.

questions.text: A patient with a central nervous system disorder is maintained on the drug alpha methyl dopa. Haemolytic anaemia develops which resolves shortly after the drug is withdrawn. Which type of hypersensitivity reactions is responsible for this immune reaction?
questions.explanation: Methyldopa-associated hemolysis is conventionally antibody-mediated type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity, unlike IgE or immune-complex disease.

questions.text: Regarding interleukins, what is the CORRECT of the following?
options: IL-2 is produced mainly by CD8+ cells
IL-10 stimulates the growth of haemopoietic stem cells
IL-4 increases the production of IL-1
IL-6 stimulates acute phase protein synthesis
IFN gamma is responsible for IgE antibody switch
questions.explanation: IL-6 induces acute-phase protein synthesis; IL-2 is chiefly T-cell-derived growth cytokine and IFN-γ does not drive IgE switching.

questions.text: What are the mediators of immune defense that attack viruses and bacteria in body fluids?
questions.explanation: Antibodies act on free microbes in body fluids; T/NK cells chiefly target host cells.

questions.text: Which of the following characterized humoral immune response to T dependent antigens?
options: Antigen is not processed by macrophage
questions.explanation: T-dependent humoral immunity supports switching, memory and T/B collaboration; it is not IgM-only or B-cell-only activation.

questions.text: Which of the following cells are activated in T-independent immune response?
questions.explanation: T-independent antigens activate B-cell antibody responses without T helper engagement.

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT belongs to innate immune responses?
questions.explanation: Class switching is adaptive B-cell differentiation; acute-phase proteins, inflammation, complement and phagocytosis are innate.

questions.text: Which of the following is caused by defective isotype immunoglobulin switching?
questions.explanation: Hyper-IgM reflects defective class switching; XLA blocks B-cell maturation and other listed defects target different compartments.

questions.text: Which of the following is correct regarding immune response to tumor?
options: Destruction of tumor cells by phagocytic cells
questions.explanation: Tumor-directed immunity can involve CTLs, ADCC, antibody complement and phagocytes.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a function of immunoglobulins?
questions.explanation: Antibody neutralizes/opsonizes and recruits complement/ADCC; presenting antigen to T cells is an APC/MHC function.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT present on B lymphocyte?
questions.explanation: CD3 is part of the TCR complex; B cells carry surface Ig, MHC-I/II and cytokine receptors.

questions.text: Which of the following substances can be recognized by PRR on macrophages
questions.explanation: LPS is a microbial pattern detected by PRRs; IL-10, C5a, lysozyme and granzymes are host molecules.

questions.text: Which one of the following factors characterizes the immune deficiency in chronic granulomatous disease?
options: Reduced levels of the third component of complement (C3)
Inability of polymorphonuclear leukocytes to kill ingested bacteria
questions.explanation: CGD impairs oxidative microbe killing after phagocytosis; C3, C1 inhibitor, antibodies and γ-chain defects define other disorders.

questions.text: Which type of immunity is offered with immune serum?
questions.explanation: Immune serum transfers preformed antibody artificially and gives passive, temporary protection.
